reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: Authors have clearly resolved all of my concerns in the revised manuscript. However, I strongly suggest that authors should add references to the revised line 272~288 (that correspond to Q#2) to provide clarity to the readers.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: I have been asked to review this manuscript after preliminary revision due to the withdrawal of review #2. The manuscript by Ji et al. describes twelve cryo-EM assemblies in detergent micelles of engineered apelin receptor with two different (non-physiological) agonists (AMG986 and JN241-9) with and without engineered Galphai/Beta1/gamma2 heterotrimer. The authors then use these twelve assemblies to construct a narrative on possible conformational transitions for the apelin receptor during activation. They use the molecular snapshots provided by these cryo-EM assemblies to argue for a particular reaction pathway. There is no way to know whether the proposed relationship between the reported assemblies represents the pathway that occurs in their highly reconstituted and engineered system, much less in either a recombinant cellular setting or physiologically. The supporting cell-based assay data is heavily normalized (minimum 2 normalization steps), which hampers independent assessment by the reader, and in several cases lacks appropriate controls to allow interpretation. Throughout, the findings from their cryo-EM assemblies are referred to as if they represent some physiological ground truth, which is a serious, unsupported, over-interpretation. I urge the authors to apply a much more conservative interpretation of their data. I also note that the novelty of the manuscript is undermined by existing publications of apelin receptor structures reported elsewhere, including by these authors. I would strongly suggest that the term “aggregation”, which the authors appear to use to mean dimerization / oligomerization should be replaced with either of these terms. Aggregation has a specific meaning in biochemistry, which is: the accumulation of misfolded or intrinsically disordered proteins into (typically) insoluble, non-functional complexes. Understanding whether GPCRs (outside Class C) do form dimers in physiological settings, and if they do, what the functional consequence is, remains an unresolved question in the field. Unfortunately, the field is largely divided into dogmatic camps of “GPCR dimerization is a general phenomenon with important physiological outcomes” and “GPCR dimerization is an artefact, with no relevance at all”. Despite the large amount of literature on the subject, conclusions remain equivocal, due to a fairly large body of literature that relies on transfected cell studies using various proximity measures that are not powered to detect the difference between close proximity and protein:protein interaction AND the difficulty in performing definitive experiments in physiologically meaningful settings. There is no teleological reason to believe GPCRs form dimers, unlike nuclear hormone receptors (dimerization required for DNA binding), receptor tyrosine kinases (dimerization required for transphosphorylation) or enzymes (dimerization provides positive or negative allostery to enable physiologically relevant sensitivity to changes in substrate availability). On the other hand, it is attractive to think that novel behaviors could emerge through the formation of GPCR heterodimers (although there is much evidence, particularly from the 1990’s to suggest signal crosstalk as a mechanism for new behaviors). In this setting, new publications on either side of this debate ought to be subject to careful critical analysis. Introduction: Page 2, lines 37-40 “GPCRs serve as central hubs in cellular signal transduction, ensuring the complexity and precision of downstream signaling through their structural versatility, characterized by diverse aggregated forms and dynamic conformational changes.” This is a meaningless word-salad, adding nothing to the paper. I would recommend removing. Page 2, lines 41-42 “Class A GPCRs exist in a dynamic equilibrium between monomeric and oligomeric forms”. Of the data cited none provide evidence for a dynamic equilibria between oligomeric states, a single figure in reference 6 (figure 3) has data that supports the contention that oxytocin receptors may form dimers in native tissue. The remainder of the citations rely on data that have alternative interpretations. I am concerned that there is an uncritical perpetuation of data over-interpretation supported by poor-quality and often careless experiments. Here are alternative interpretations for the common experimental types presented in these figures: • Co-immunoprecipitation. With the inclusion of all relevant controls (particularly for membrane proteins that have a propensity to aggregate), co-immunoprecipitation should only be used to conclude that 2 proteins are present as part of a complex, direct interaction cannot be concluded. Absence of data from native tissue should be viewed with scepticism. Antibodies for GPCRs are frequently un-specific. • Confocal microscopy showing “co-localisation”. Under standard techniques in an optimally adjusted system with a high NA objective the point-spread-function of GFP/Alexa488 is ~140 nm in the x-y and 380 nm in the z with a volume of about 4 x 10^6 nm^3 (obviously this gets bigger with longer wavelength). A typical GPCR occupies a volume of about 70 nm^3 , thus over 50,000 GPCRs can fit into a single PSF. Data is frequently reported where GPCRs do not appear to be localized to the plasma membrane, which is inconsistent with known properties. Antibodies for GPCRs are frequently un-specific. • BRET or FRET (resonance energy transfer techniques). Generally, only applicable in transfected cell studies. Relies on the assumption that direct interaction is required for resonance energy transfer. This is clearly not true, given the widespread use of bystander BRET to measure (for example) GPCR trafficking. Saturation BRET remains problematic as controls are difficult. If partner proteins for both donor and acceptor traffic to the same membrane subdomains, the readout for this assay will appear to indicate a specific interaction. Unless controls for collisional (random) BRET signals have equivalent expression (on a per-cell basis) to the test AND have comparable trafficking, interpretation is ambiguous. • Altered signalling output in the presence of a second GPCR. This could equally occur due to signal crosstalk. • Mutational analysis of putative dimerization interface (mostly TM bundle mutations, typically altering signalling output). Even if carefully controlled for expression level it is usually not possible to exclude the possibility that the mutation alters transmission of ligand binding event through the GPCR to its intracellular partner. Page 3 ,lines 52-55 “….supported by single-molecule imaging that confirms dimeric formation, and it is the first Class A GPCR whose stable dimeric structures have been captured by cryo-EM^8,15,16.” Reference 8 is provided to the contention that apelin receptor can interchange between dimers and monomers in cells (including using single molecule imaging). This reference is problematic, clustering (single molecule experiments, figure 1) lack appropriate controls (e.g. monomeric cell-surface receptor). If taken at face value, there is no equivalence between clustering and dimerization, this is below the resolution of the experiment. Even if dimerization is accepted there is not necessarily and equivalence between physical co-localisation and functional dimerization. Figure 2a, heavily cropped and manipulated western blots, non-equivalent loading of “mix” control, full blots not provided in supplementary information. Panels 2b&c are much more problematic, Oxytocin receptor is used as a ‘negative’ control in BRET experiments (i.e. as a receptor that does not dimerise), this is despite the fact that Reference 5 specifically demonstrates oxytocin receptor dimers by both FRET (weak evidence) but also by ligand allostery on native membranes (strong evidence), dimerization of oxytocin receptor is also reported in PMID: 27420737. Figure 3 & 4, no negative OR positive controls with both donor and acceptor included. Figure 5 uses interference peptides to infer TM1,2,3 & 4 as parts of the dimerization interface, this conflicts with data from PMID 35817871 (e.g. 7W0L) where TM4 plays no part and TM2 has only a single residue within a distance that could support an interaction (also noting that this is consistent with the present publication) bringing into question this methodology. The remaining figures also lack appropriate controls. I would suggest rephrasing to more accurately reflect the ambiguity of data: “APLNR is a model system that may be suitable for investigating the dynamic transition between monomeric and dimeric forms of class A GPCR, supported by transfected cell studies, and cryo-EM^8,15,16.” The clinical trial and published data on AMG986/Azelaprag is presented in a way that the reader might think that biased agonism and/or dimeric/monomeric receptor signalling profile is the reason for the clinical trial discontinuation (page 3, lines 71-74): “However, a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating AMG986 was recently discontinued owing to potential adverse effects, highlighting the necessity to explore its molecular mechanism in stimulating various apelin receptor forms.” This does not seem to be the most parsimonious interpretation as the clinical trial was terminated due to ~5% of patients in the Azelaprag arm having blood markers consistent with liver toxicity (no patients in control arm). The size of the trial suggests that this is, in fact, an Azelaprag side effect, however the most likely cause is off-target liver toxicity, not an undesirable on-target effect, as implied by the authors. I suggest removing the second half of this sentence and replace with: ““However, a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating AMG986 was recently discontinued owing to potential off-target liver toxicity.” No observation of transitions between different conformations is made in this manuscript. This would require NMR, single molecule FRET or HDX-MS (if the transitions are slow enough), or MD-simulations could be conducted to model transitions. None of these are performed in this manuscript, only static snapshots are determined with no way of knowing whether these occur in a particular order on a reaction pathway OR whether some are off-pathway conformations. Page 4, lines 85-87: “We therefore directly observed the stepwise transition and conformational changes of APLNR dimers towards monomers from the apo to the active state.” I suggest rephrasing to: “We therefore directly observed a range of conformational states of APLNR dimers and monomers, both apo and active states, which provide potential pathways for conformational transition between these states.” Results: Page 4, line 96 “…. network formed by F101^3.24 plays a …..” Here I assume the 3.24 refers to the Ballesteros-Weinstein numbering system for TM helices of GPCRs, please explain this to the reader and include the appropriate reference. I suggest “…. network formed by F101^3.24 (where the superscript refers to the Ballesteros-Weinstein transmembrane numbering system (ref)) plays a …..”. Reference is: Ballesteros, J.A., and Weinstein, H. (1995). Integrated methods for the construction of three-dimensional models and computational probing of structure-function relations in G protein-coupled receptors. Methods Neurosci. 25, 366–428. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1043-9471(05)80049-7. Page 4, lines 102-104: “AMG986 showed roughly 10-fold greater potency in activating various G-proteins, including Gi, Gq and G13, as well as β-arrestin, compared to JN241-9.” Please provide statistical analysis to support this difference. The appropriate analysis is to derive the pEC50 from each biological repeat, use this to derive a mean and error then test for difference between pEC50s (one-way ANOVA). It is more appropriate to display SD rather than SEM, since the former is an estimate of the biological variance. I note that supplemental file “583494_1_related_ms_11086941_sz33ll” contains individual columns that appear to sum to the total of technical replicates multiplied by biological repeats. Could the authors please confirm that they have no conflated technical and biological replicates? While Nature Communications makes no formal recommendation on use of error bars (see: https://www.nature.com/collections/qghhqm and https://www.nature.com/articles/nmeth.2659), best practice for this type of data would be SD. I also note that the double normalisation (individual baseline normalization, followed by conversion to fold over baseline, followed by conversion to % of WT-AMG896 Emax) has the potential to obscure differences in G protein activation whilst also potentially accentuating differences between ligands. I would prefer to see data where the final normalization step is removed. Page 4/5, lines 105-106. “Additionally, AMG986 induced a more rapid activation rate than JN241-9 (Supplementary Fig. 1d).” Firstly, please comment on the magnitude of difference, looking at the data this is very small and is hard to envision why one would think this is of any biological relevance. Secondly, please provide analysis to support that this difference is statistically significant. Third, as with the above comment, I suggest SD. The axis of supp fig 1d is labelled “cAMP accumulation %”, this is the % of what? For all cAMP data, are the authors confident that sensor has not been saturated? For example, was a cell permeant cAMP analoge (e.g. 8-CPT) included at the end of the assay? Page 5, lines 107-108. “Though negligible differences in EC50 or Emax from G-protein signaling, the dimer-reduced form (F1013.24A) showed a higher Emax than the dimeric form in the β-arrestin signaling (Supplementary Fig. 1f).” Please refer to the magnitude of change and also provide analysis supporting a statistically significant difference. Without experiments performed under parallel conditions to quantitate cell-surface expression this change in Emax could be as a result of altered receptor number. Elsewhere (supp fig 8) the authors report cell surface expression by ELISA, however it is not clear from the methods that this was performed under equivalent transfection conditions to the β-arrestin assay. It is not clear from the methods whether cell integrity would be maintained using the fixation technique used and no negative control is included. As this data stands, interpretation is ambiguous. I suggest a cautious interpretation of this result: “Though negligible differences in EC50 or Emax from G-protein signaling, the dimer-reduced form (F1013.24A) showed a higher Emax than the dimeric form in the β-arrestin signaling (Supplementary Fig. 1f), consistent with previous results^15, which may be indicative that the dimer exhibits G-protein bias compared to the monomer.” The apparent unity hill-slope of both cAMP and β-arrestin responses has no detectable change between the WT receptor and the F101A mutant (proposed monomeric form), nor does there appear to be a detectable change in pEC50. This suggests that in the dimeric form of the apelin receptor, there is no detectable co-operativity (negative or positive) for either ligand. Thermodynamically, it is hard to envision how dimerization would NOT alter ligand binding (see REF 6 and Birdsall, N.J.M. (2010). Class A GPCR heterodimers: evidence from binding studies. Trends Pharmacol. Sci. 31, 499–508. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tips.2010.08.003.). A statement to this effect should be included immediately after the above sentence: “No detectable change in either Hill-slope or pEC50 is evident for either AMG986 or JN241-9 between WT and monomeric (F101A) receptors, suggesting that ligand binding allostery, if present, is not detectable.” Page 5 lines 110-112. “Moreover, cAMP accumulation results showed that the dimer-reduced form exhibits higher constitutive activity than that of dimeric form (Supplementary Figs. 1d-e).” Please refer to the magnitude of change and also provide analysis supporting a statistically significant difference. I would also suggest softening this statement, as without data showing that receptor expression is equivalent AND that the WT v’s F101A mutant do not alter (for example) adenylate cyclase or phosphodiesterase expression it is not possible to attribute the change in baseline to receptor constitutive activity. A solution would be to perform assays using an inverse agonist for Apelin receptor, although I am not aware of one. I would suggest the following: “Moreover, cAMP accumulation results showed that the dimer-reduced form appear to exhibit ~25% higher constitutive activity than that of dimeric form (Supplementary Figs. 1d-e, p<0.ABC).” The curve for used for these concentration-response curves is not stated, either in the results or in the methods. Please include the equation used in the methods section. If a 3 parameter logistic equation has been used, this should be justified as it would fail to take into account 2:2 stoichiometry. Page 5, line 120-122. “Here, we successfully achieved high-resolution cryo-EM structures of agonists-bound class A GPCR in various conformations without G-protein, delineating the dynamic process of activation.” Again, these are snapshots and there is no data that addresses whether they are all on the reaction pathway and if they are which order they occur. I suggest a more conservative interpretation of this data: “Here, we successfully achieved high-resolution cryo-EM structures of agonists-bound class A GPCR in various conformations without G-protein, providing potential insights into the dynamic process of activation.” Page 5, line 127. “Fortunately, we identified ….” Fortunately is unnecessary and pejorative, I suggest to start the sentence “We identified …..” Page 5, lines 133-135. “Additionally, the two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein are distinguished by unique conformational changes of TM6 and helix 8 (H8) in one protomer (termed by LBS2a and LBS2b, respectively) (Supplementary Fig. 2b).” Conformation changes are assumed not measured, these are snapshots and there is no reason to believe they represent a particular reaction co-ordinate. I suggest: “Additionally, the two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein are distinguished by unique conformations of TM6 and helix 8 (H8) in one protomer (termed by LBS2a and LBS2b, respectively) (Supplementary Fig. 2b).” Page 6, lines 136-137. “These results indicate that the conformations are in a ligand-dependent manner.” This sentence doesn’t make sense in English, I suggest: “These results indicate that the different ligands may select different conformational states.” Page 6, lines 143-146. “Data processing revealed that AMG986-bound dimeric APLNR–Gi1 complexes adopt two conformations in protB (termed by ACT2a and ACT2b, respectively), aligning with those structures without G-protein (Supplementary Fig. 3b).” is there meant to be an alignment between G-protein free and G-protein bound complexes in Supp Fig 3b? I don’t see one? Page 6, lines 149-151. “To elucidate the structural transition of APLNR from its apo to active state, we first compared two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein (LBS2a and LBS2b) against the apo state to identify structural differences (Fig.2a)”. Implicit in this analysis is the assumption that the reaction co-ordinate for a GPCR to lower the energy barrier for nucleotide exchange at its cognate G protein involves binding of the agonist prior to binding of the G protein. What is the evidence that this is the case for the Apelin Receptor? The majority of Class A GPCRs where agonist binding has been studied such that G protein-coupling can be modulated by the addition of non-hydrolysable GTP analogues show that the high affinity state is one in which the G protein is engaged with the receptor. There are a range of Class A receptors where there is evidence of pre-coupling of G protein to receptor. Implicit in the ternary complex model is that G protein coupling may occur prior to agonist binding. Where is has been studied, apo GPCRs explore conformations that are either intermediate to activation or similar to fully active (ternary) conformations. Lastly, large scale MD simulations of many Class A GPCRs (including the Apelin receptor) supports the notion that these receptors explore active-like states in the absence of agonist binding. Taken together, and in the absence of data that supports agonist binding first, I think it is faulty logic to ascribe the agonist bound, G protein free state as a transition to the active state. It could be this, but it could also be a state that is not on the reaction pathway. Seed references are below: 1. Aranda-García, D., Stepniewski, T.M., Torrens-Fontanals, M. et al. Large scale investigation of GPCR molecular dynamics data uncovers allosteric sites and lateral gateways. Nat Commun 16, 2020 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57034-y 2. Kim TH, Chung KY, Manglik A, Hansen AL, Dror RO, Mildorf TJ, Shaw DE, Kobilka BK, Prosser RS. The role of ligands on the equilibria between functional states of a G protein-coupled receptor. J Am Chem Soc. 2013 Jun 26;135(25):9465-74. doi: 10.1021/ja404305k. Epub 2013 Jun 14. PMID: 23721409; PMCID: PMC3763947. 3. Nobles M, Benians A, Tinker A. Heterotrimeric G proteins precouple with G protein-coupled receptors in living cells. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2005 Dec 20;102(51):18706-11. doi: 10.1073/pnas.0504778102. Epub 2005 Dec 13. PMID: 16352729; PMCID: PMC1317907. 4. De Lean A, Stadel JM, Lefkowitz RJ. A ternary complex model explains the agonist-specific binding properties of the adenylate cyclase-coupled beta-adrenergic receptor. J Biol Chem. 1980 Aug 10;255(15):7108-17. PMID: 6248546. Figure 2 and supplementary figure 4. There are a number of relatively subtle changes in side chain position/rotation that are ascribed as being part of the activation pathway. The apparent resolution of the relevant parts of the receptor appears to be between 2 and 2.2A (supp fig 2 and 3), which should allow good confidence in assigning these. The maps on which these models are based and the models themselves are not provided (or perhaps I can’t find them?), so it is not possible as a reviewer to independently verify the side-chain movements being presented. I could not find an editorial policy on making these data (maps and models) available to reviewers, but this would be best-practice. Page 7, line 178. “Surprisingly, we observed ….”. No need for the pejorative surprising. Present the data and let the reader judge whether it is “surprising”. Page 7/8 lines 194-197. “These findings indicate that AMG986 can independently induce activation of a single protomer within the APLNR dimer, in contrast to JN241-9, which necessitates G-protein engagement for receptor activation.” These are snapshots of dynamic complexes and it is not clear that induced fit is in operation, I would encourage more cautious interpretation. I also note that if the authors interpretation is correct, one would predict that AMG986 would possess higher efficacy compared with JN241-9. I see no evidence of this. Pages 8 & 9. Section entitled: “G-protein coupled activation of APLNR facilitates the dimer-to-monomer transition” again, order of events is not known, it could be that dimer to monomer transition occurs first then G protein binding occurs then agonist binding occurs (or pretty much any other variation on this). Please apply a more cautious approach to interpretation OR provide evidence from an endogenous setting that supports one or other orders for the reaction pathway. Page 9, lines 236-240. “Furthermore, the kinetic GloSensor cAMP assay revealed that signaling response associated with monomeric activation (F101A) was greater than that of the dimeric form (WT) during the initial 15 minutes. However, both responses converged thereafter, further suggesting that most dimers transition into monomers upon receptor activation.” Please quantitate the difference in reaction rate and perform statistics to support that this. If this data quantitively and statistically supports faster cAMP inhibition kinetics if could be interpreted that the F101A mutant has higher propensity to pre-couple to its cognate G protein, thus increasing the agonist on-rate and subsequent Gi/o activation. Page 9, line 244. “Intriguingly, the ….” Please remove “intriguingly”. Page 10 & 11, section entitled “The extent of dimer dissociation upon APLNR activation is ligand-dependent”, once again, please apply a more conservative interpretation of the data. Page 10, lines 260-262. “These findings suggest that ligand-specific modulation of dimeric conformations may contributes to varying degrees of dimer dissociation upon activation.” Previously the authors imply that transition to the monomeric state enhances the rate of signalling, yet they do not assess whether the rate of signalling is differentially altered for the two ligands, which might be expected. Could the authors please comment? Figure 4c. The depletion of cholesterol from cells could conceivably alter availability of the G protein to the receptor and/or activity of adenylate cyclase (most isoforms are integral membrane proteins). As a minimum, the authors need to provide parallel experiments where the effect of cholesterol depletion on basal adenylate cyclase activity is assesses in cells that do not express the apelin receptor. Discussion should be rewritten with a more conservative interpretation of the data. I have been asked to comment on whether the authors have adequately addressed the comments by reviewer 2. On balance they have done a good job of this.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5: I like to congratulate the authors for a very interesting and conclusive manuscript. All the concerns of Reviewer 2 have been addressed by the authors in their rebuttal letter. Except for the last point (how common might by the dimer/monomer transition observed for APLNR for class A and class B receptors?) the authors accordingly included changes in the manuscript. I would recommend adding a short statement in the discussion section addressing the above mentioned question. I enjoyed reading the manuscript and found only one additional point, not mentioned by the reviewers so far that in my opinion is so important that it needs clarification: To be sure that cholesterol depletion increases basal activity of APLNR it is necessary to show in the absence of APLNR how much cholesterol depletion affects forskolin-induced cAMP accumulation. Only if cholesterol depletion reduces cAMP accumulation to larger extent in APLNR expressing cells compared to non-APLNR expressing cells we can be sure that the results reflect an increase in basal activity of the receptor. Minor point: there is a little flaw in the figure legend of Fig. 4d: Dose-response curves for AMG986-induced cAMP accumulation in WT and F1013.24A….. If I’m correct, it should state: Concentration-response curves for the AMG986-mediated inhibition of forskolin-induced CAMP accumulations in WT and F1013.24A, …..

peer_review_rounds.author_response: We thank the referees for their valuable time in reviewing our manuscript and the constructive suggestions that they have provided. We have carefully taken these comments into consideration in preparing a revised version of our manuscript. Please find below a point-by-point response to the referees with our responses in blue and the reviewers’ comments in black. Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author): Authors have clearly resolved all of my concerns in the revised manuscript. However, I strongly suggest that authors should add references to the revised line 272~288 (that correspond to Q#2) to provide clarity to the readers. Response: We thank the reviewer for the helpful comments, which have helped us improve the manuscript. We have added the relevant references in the corresponding sections as follows: “To date, multiple agonist-bound APLNR dimer structures in the presence or absence of G-protein have been resolved1,2. Accordingly, we compared the APLNR structures resolved in this study with previously reported structures. Pairwise alignment of the entire dimeric assemblies revealed relatively small Cα root mean square deviation (RMSD) values (<1.0 Å) among G-protein-free dimers (Supplementary Fig. 7a). In contrast, Cα RMSDs between structures with and without G-protein coupling exhibited larger deviations (1.0 to 2.5 Å), largely attributable to conformational shifts in TM6 and H8 (Supplementary Fig. 7a). Moreover, Cα RMSDs among G-protein-coupling dimers also showed relatively larger deviations (1.0 to 2.1 Å), suggesting that different ligands induce distinct dimer conformations in the active state (Supplementary Fig. 7a). To assess the extent of dimer dissociation, we compared the Cα RMSDs of protB aligned on protA (Supplementary Fig. 7b). Comparison between G-protein-bound and G-protein-free dimers revealed a remarkably wide range of Cα RMSDs (2.3 to 6.3 Å), particularly in comparisons involving the ELA–Gi complex (PDB: 7W0N)1, further indicating different ligands induce varying degrees of dimer dissociation during activation (Supplementary Figs. 7b-d).” Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author): I have been asked to review this manuscript after preliminary revision due to the withdrawal of review #2. The manuscript by Ji et al. describes twelve cryo-EM assemblies in detergent micelles of engineered apelin receptor with two different (non-physiological) agonists (AMG986 and JN241-9) with and without engineered Galphai/Beta1/gamma2 heterotrimer. The authors then use these twelve assemblies to construct a narrative on possible conformational transitions for the apelin receptor during activation. They use the molecular snapshots provided by these cryo-EM assemblies to argue for a particular reaction pathway. There is no way to know whether the proposed relationship between the reported assemblies represents the pathway that occurs in their highly reconstituted and engineered system, much less in either a recombinant cellular setting or physiologically. The supporting cell-based assay data is heavily normalized (minimum 2 normalization steps), which hampers independent assessment by the reader, and in several cases lacks appropriate controls to allow interpretation. Throughout, the findings from their cryo-EM assemblies are referred to as if they represent some physiological ground truth, which is a serious, unsupported, over-interpretation. I urge the authors to apply a much more conservative interpretation of their data. I also note that the novelty of the manuscript is undermined by existing publications of apelin receptor structures reported elsewhere, including by these authors. Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this thoughtful critique and agree that our structural findings should be interpreted with greater caution. In response, we have carefully revised the manuscript to moderate statements that may have overstated the physiological relevance of our results. Specifically, definitive statements regarding “the” activation pathway have been replaced with more conservative interpretation such as “potential conformational transitions” observed in our experimental system. While we acknowledge the inherent limitations of our engineered and reconstituted system, the twelve cryo-EM structures obtained under various ligand and G-protein conditions provide a unique series of molecular snapshots. Furthermore, these static snapshots are complemented by time-dependent signaling assays, which provide correlative evidence of the dynamic transition process. Within this in vitro framework, the combined data reveal a continuum of conformational states, allowing us to propose a plausible model for dynamic monomer-dimer transition in ligand-induced apelin receptor activation at atomic resolution. Rather than defining a universal physiological pathway, our objective is to generate testable hypotheses and mechanistic insights based on the structural and functional diversity we have observed. 1. I would strongly suggest that the term “aggregation”, which the authors appear to use to mean dimerization / oligomerization should be replaced with either of these terms. Aggregation has a specific meaning in biochemistry, which is: the accumulation of misfolded or intrinsically disordered proteins into (typically) insoluble, non-functional complexes. Response: The reviewer is correct to highlight this critical distinction in biochemical terminology. We sincerely appreciate the feedback and have revised the manuscript accordingly. The term “aggregation” has been replaced with “dimerization/oligomerization” to properly describe the specific protein-protein interactions observed in our study. Understanding whether GPCRs (outside Class C) do form dimers in physiological settings, and if they do, what the functional consequence is, remains an unresolved question in the field. Unfortunately, the field is largely divided into dogmatic camps of “GPCR dimerization is a general phenomenon with important physiological outcomes” and “GPCR dimerization is an artefact, with no relevance at all”. Despite the large amount of literature on the subject, conclusions remain equivocal, due to a fairly large body of literature that relies on transfected cell studies using various proximity measures that are not powered to detect the difference between close proximity and protein:protein interaction AND the difficulty in performing definitive experiments in physiologically meaningful settings. There is no teleological reason to believe GPCRs form dimers, unlike nuclear hormone receptors (dimerization required for DNA binding), receptor tyrosine kinases (dimerization required for transphosphorylation) or enzymes (dimerization provides positive or negative allostery to enable physiologically relevant sensitivity to changes in substrate availability). On the other hand, it is attractive to think that novel behaviors could emerge through the formation of GPCR heterodimers (although there is much evidence, particularly from the 1990’s to suggest signal crosstalk as a mechanism for new behaviors). In this setting, new publications on either side of this debate ought to be subject to careful critical analysis. 2. Introduction: Page 2, lines 37-40 “GPCRs serve as central hubs in cellular signal transduction, ensuring the complexity and precision of downstream signaling through their structural versatility, characterized by diverse aggregated forms and dynamic conformational changes.” This is a meaningless word-salad, adding nothing to the paper. I would recommend removing. Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. Following your suggestion, the manuscript has been revised to remove this sentence. 3. Page 2, lines 41-42 “Class A GPCRs exist in a dynamic equilibrium between monomeric and oligomeric forms”. Of the data cited none provide evidence for a dynamic equilibria between oligomeric states, a single figure in reference 6 (figure 3) has data that supports the contention that oxytocin receptors may form dimers in native tissue. The remainder of the citations rely on data that have alternative interpretations. I am concerned that there is an uncritical perpetuation of data over-interpretation supported by poor-quality and often careless experiments. Here are alternative interpretations for the common experimental types presented in these figures: • Co-immunoprecipitation. With the inclusion of all relevant controls (particularly for membrane proteins that have a propensity to aggregate), co-immunoprecipitation should only be used to conclude that 2 proteins are present as part of a complex, direct interaction cannot be concluded. Absence of data from native tissue should be viewed with scepticism. Antibodies for GPCRs are frequently un-specific. • Confocal microscopy showing “co-localisation”. Under standard techniques in an optimally adjusted system with a high NA objective the point-spread-function of GFP/Alexa488 is ~140 nm in the x-y and 380 nm in the z with a volume of about 4 x 10^6 nm^3 (obviously this gets bigger with longer wavelength). A typical GPCR occupies a volume of about 70 nm^3 , thus over 50,000 GPCRs can fit into a single PSF. Data is frequently reported where GPCRs do not appear to be localized to the plasma membrane, which is inconsistent with known properties. Antibodies for GPCRs are frequently un-specific. • BRET or FRET (resonance energy transfer techniques). Generally, only applicable in transfected cell studies. Relies on the assumption that direct interaction is required for resonance energy transfer. This is clearly not true, given the widespread use of bystander BRET to measure (for example) GPCR trafficking. Saturation BRET remains problematic as controls are difficult. If partner proteins for both donor and acceptor traffic to the same membrane subdomains, the readout for this assay will appear to indicate a specific interaction. Unless controls for collisional (random) BRET signals have equivalent expression (on a per-cell basis) to the test AND have comparable trafficking, interpretation is ambiguous. • Altered signalling output in the presence of a second GPCR. This could equally occur due to signal crosstalk. • Mutational analysis of putative dimerization interface (mostly TM bundle mutations, typically altering signalling output). Even if carefully controlled for expression level it is usually not possible to exclude the possibility that the mutation alters transmission of ligand binding event through the GPCR to its intracellular partner. Response: We thank the reviewer for their critical assessment, which has allowed us to significantly enhance our work. We agree that our original statement was an overgeneralization of the cited literature. Accordingly, we have revised the sentence to ensure greater precision and alignment with the published evidence as follows: “While Class C GPCRs are obligate dimers for their function, Class A GPCRs may exist as monomers or oligomers3-8, exhibiting distinct agonist affinity, efficacy, as well as the signaling profiles and pharmacological functions9-12.” 4. Page 3 ,lines 52-55 “….supported by single-molecule imaging that confirms dimeric formation, and it is the first Class A GPCR whose stable dimeric structures have been captured by cryo-EM^8,15,16.” Reference 8 is provided to the contention that apelin receptor can interchange between dimers and monomers in cells (including using single molecule imaging). This reference is problematic, clustering (single molecule experiments, figure 1) lack appropriate controls (e.g. monomeric cell-surface receptor). If taken at face value, there is no equivalence between clustering and dimerization, this is below the resolution of the experiment. Even if dimerization is accepted there is not necessarily and equivalence between physical co-localisation and functional dimerization. Figure 2a, heavily cropped and manipulated western blots, non-equivalent loading of “mix” control, full blots not provided in supplementary information. Panels 2b&c are much more problematic, Oxytocin receptor is used as a ‘negative’ control in BRET experiments (i.e. as a receptor that does not dimerise), this is despite the fact that Reference 5 specifically demonstrates oxytocin receptor dimers by both FRET (weak evidence) but also by ligand allostery on native membranes (strong evidence), dimerization of oxytocin receptor is also reported in PMID: 27420737. Figure 3 & 4, no negative OR positive controls with both donor and acceptor included. Figure 5 uses interference peptides to infer TM1,2,3 & 4 as parts of the dimerization interface, this conflicts with data from PMID 35817871 (e.g. 7W0L) where TM4 plays no part and TM2 has only a single residue within a distance that could support an interaction (also noting that this is consistent with the present publication) bringing into question this methodology. The remaining figures also lack appropriate controls. I would suggest rephrasing to more accurately reflect the ambiguity of data: “APLNR is a model system that may be suitable for investigating the dynamic transition between monomeric and dimeric forms of class A GPCR, supported by transfected cell studies, and cryo-EM^8,15,16.” Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. We have revised the manuscript accordingly as follows: “APLNR is a model system that may be suitable for investigating the dynamic transition between monomeric and dimeric forms of class A GPCR, supported by both transfected cell studies and cryo-EM structures1,2,6.” 5. The clinical trial and published data on AMG986/Azelaprag is presented in a way that the reader might think that biased agonism and/or dimeric/monomeric receptor signalling profile is the reason for the clinical trial discontinuation (page 3, lines 71-74): “However, a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating AMG986 was recently discontinued owing to potential adverse effects, highlighting the necessity to explore its molecular mechanism in stimulating various apelin receptor forms.” This does not seem to be the most parsimonious interpretation as the clinical trial was terminated due to ~5% of patients in the Azelaprag arm having blood markers consistent with liver toxicity (no patients in control arm). The size of the trial suggests that this is, in fact, an Azelaprag side effect, however the most likely cause is off-target liver toxicity, not an undesirable on-target effect, as implied by the authors. I suggest removing the second half of this sentence and replace with: ““However, a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating AMG986 was recently discontinued owing to potential off-target liver toxicity.” Response: We thank the reviewer for raising these important points. We have revised the manuscript accordingly as follows: “However, a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating AMG986 was recently discontinued owing to potential off-target liver toxicity.” 6. No observation of transitions between different conformations is made in this manuscript. This would require NMR, single molecule FRET or HDX-MS (if the transitions are slow enough), or MD-simulations could be conducted to model transitions. None of these are performed in this manuscript, only static snapshots are determined with no way of knowing whether these occur in a particular order on a reaction pathway OR whether some are off-pathway conformations. Page 4, lines 85-87: “We therefore directly observed the stepwise transition and conformational changes of APLNR dimers towards monomers from the apo to the active state.” I suggest rephrasing to: “We therefore directly observed a range of conformational states of APLNR dimers and monomers, both apo and active states, which provide potential pathways for conformational transition between these states.” Response: We thank the reviewer for the insightful feedback. We have revised the manuscript accordingly as follows: “We therefore directly observed a range of conformational states of APLNR dimers and monomers, both apo and active states, which provide potential pathways for conformational transition between these states.” 7. Results: Page 4, line 96 “…. network formed by F101^3.24 plays a …..” Here I assume the 3.24 refers to the Ballesteros-Weinstein numbering system for TM helices of GPCRs, please explain this to the reader and include the appropriate reference. I suggest “…. network formed by F101^3.24 (where the superscript refers to the Ballesteros-Weinstein transmembrane numbering system (ref)) plays a …..”. Reference is: Ballesteros, J.A., and Weinstein, H. (1995). Integrated methods for the construction of three-dimensional models and computational probing of structure-function relations in G protein-coupled receptors. Methods Neurosci. 25, 366–428. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1043-9471(05)80049-7. Response: We appreciate the reviewer's careful reading and astute observations. In response, we have revised the manuscript as follows: “Previous structural studies of the APLNR have indicated that the π-π interactions network formed by F1013.24 (where the superscript refers to the Ballesteros-Weinstein transmembrane numbering system13) plays a central role in stabilizing the dimeric interface1.” 8. Page 4, lines 102-104: “AMG986 showed roughly 10-fold greater potency in activating various G-proteins, including Gi, Gq and G13, as well as β-arrestin, compared to JN241-9.” Please provide statistical analysis to support this difference. The appropriate analysis is to derive the pEC50 from each biological repeat, use this to derive a mean and error then test for difference between pEC50s (one-way ANOVA). It is more appropriate to display SD rather than SEM, since the former is an estimate of the biological variance. I note that supplemental file “583494_1_related_ms_11086941_sz33ll” contains individual columns that appear to sum to the total of technical replicates multiplied by biological repeats. Could the authors please confirm that they have no conflated technical and biological replicates? While Nature Communications makes no formal recommendation on use of error bars (see:https://www.nature.com/collections/qghhqmandhttps://www.nature.com/articles/nmeth.2659), best practice for this type of data would be SD. I also note that the double normalisation (individual baseline normalization, followed by conversion to fold over baseline, followed by conversion to % of WT-AMG896 Emax) has the potential to obscure differences in G protein activation whilst also potentially accentuating differences between ligands. I would prefer to see data where the final normalization step is removed. Response: We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments regarding the statistical analysis and data normalization for the potency comparison between AMG986 and JN241-9. We have carefully considered the points raised and provide the following clarifications: 1. The reviewer emphasizes the importance of robust statistical analysis. As suggested, we have now performed a formal statistical comparison of the pEC values derived 50 from individual biological replicates (n ≥ 3). This analysis, conducted using one-way ANOVA, confirms that the difference in potency between AMG986 and JN241-9 is statistically significant (p < 0.05), thereby quantitatively supporting the stated ~10-fold difference (Fig. R1). Furthermore, the source data have been provided as part of our submission, in full compliance with the Nature Communications policy on source data (https://www.nature.com/ncomms/submit/how-to-submit). 2. We appreciate the reviewer’s note on error bars. We chose to present the data as the mean ± SEM (Standard Error of the Mean) for the following reason: The primary goal of our experiment was to estimate and compare the mean potency (pEC ) of the 50 ligands across our biological replicates. The SEM is a direct measure of the precision of this estimated mean and is therefore most appropriate for making inferences about the population mean from our sample. While SD accurately describes the variability within our sample, our conclusion is focused on the difference between the mean potencies of the two compounds, for which the SEM is the conventional metric. 3. Regarding the normalization strategy, we agree that the final normalization step (to % of WT-AMG986 Emax) accentuates the difference in efficacy between the ligands. This was applied to directly visualize their relative maximal signaling capabilities, a key parameter in functional pharmacology. This approach is well-established for highlighting differences in efficacy and is consistent with methodologies used in other publications1,14. Reply figure 1. Dose-response curves and pEC analysis of ligands-triggered 50 signaling pathways of APLNR. a-c, The effects of two agonists on WT and partially dimer-disrupted mutant F101A. Dose-response curves show AMG986- and JN241-9-induced G (a), G (b) and G (c) i q 13 signaling were measured by NanoBiT assay in HEK293T cells. d, Dose-response curves show the duration of cAMP signaling response induced by 10 μM of each ligand. e, Dose-response curves for AMG986- and JN241-9-induced cAMP accumulation measured by GloSensor cAMP assay in HEK293T cells. f, β-arrestin2 recruitment were measured by BRET assay. Data are presented as mean ± SEM with a minimum of three technical replicates, which were performed in triplicates each. g, The pEC values corresponding to the dose-response curves in a-c and e, f are 50 summarized. Data are presented as pEC ± SEM with a minimum of three technical 50 replicates, which were performed in triplicates each. 9. Page 4/5, lines 105-106. “Additionally, AMG986 induced a more rapid activation rate than JN241-9 (Supplementary Fig. 1d).” Firstly, please comment on the magnitude of difference, looking at the data this is very small and is hard to envision why one would think this is of any biological relevance. Secondly, please provide analysis to support that this difference is statistically significant. Third, as with the above comment, I suggest SD. The axis of supp fig 1d is labelled “cAMP accumulation %”, this is the % of what? For all cAMP data, are the authors confident that sensor has not been saturated? For example, was a cell permeant cAMP analoge (e.g. 8-CPT) included at the end of the assay? Response: We thank the reviewer for these insightful questions regarding the cAMP kinetics data in Supplementary Fig. 1d. Please find our point-by-point responses below. 1. The “cAMP accumulation (%)” represents the values normalized to the cAMP level of WT-AMG986 at the 0-minute time point, set as 100%. While the absolute numerical difference may appear modest, AMG986 consistently demonstrated a lower percentage of cAMP accumulation than JN241-9 at every measured time point. This consistent and earlier separation of the curves indicates a faster activation rate for AMG986, a characteristic we believe is biologically relevant in the context of kinetic signaling profiles. 2. We appreciate the critical point regarding sensor saturation. We are confident that the cAMP sensor was operating within its linear dynamic range throughout our experiments for the following reasons: Our assay measures G-mediated inhibition of i cAMP. We first applied Forskolin to elevate cAMP to a stable plateau, creating a wide and robust window for observing inhibitory effects. This design prevents the issue of a limited “downward range” that could occur at basal cAMP levels and ensures the upper limit of the signal is within the sensor’s range. Furthermore, the cAMP accumulation traces show distinct and statistically significant steady-state plateaus between the WT and F101A groups following ligand application. These confirms that the sensor was not saturated at the lower end of the signal and was accurately reporting ligand-mediated cAMP changes. 10. Page 5, lines 107-108. “Though negligible differences in EC50 or Emax from G-protein signaling, the dimer-reduced form (F1013.24A) showed a higher Emax than the dimeric form in the β-arrestin signaling (Supplementary Fig. 1f).” Please refer to the magnitude of change and also provide analysis supporting a statistically significant difference. Without experiments performed under parallel conditions to quantitate cell-surface expression this change in Emax could be as a result of altered receptor number. Elsewhere (supp fig 8) the authors report cell surface expression by ELISA, however it is not clear from the methods that this was performed under equivalent transfection conditions to the β-arrestin assay. It is not clear from the methods whether cell integrity would be maintained using the fixation technique used and no negative control is included. As this data stands, interpretation is ambiguous. I suggest a cautious interpretation of this result: “Though negligible differences in EC50 or Emax from G-protein signaling, the dimer-reduced form (F1013.24A) showed a higher Emax than the dimeric form in the β-arrestin signaling (Supplementary Fig. 1f), consistent with previous results^15, which may be indicative that the dimer exhibits G-protein bias compared to the monomer.” Response: We thank the reviewer for raising these important points and providing valuable suggestions. The observed greater Emax for the F1013.24A than WT in the β-arrestin recruitment assay, while modest, was a consistent and reproducible effect. Additionally, the cell-surface ELISA was performed under equivalent transfection conditions to those used in the β-arrestin assays. This assay, involving formaldehyde fixation followed by detection of GPCRs on the cell surface using specific antibodies, is a well-established and widely used method for determining cell-surface expression of GPCRs15-17. This method has been validated to preserve cell integrity and specifically label plasma membrane-localized receptors. Furthermore, we have revised the manuscript accordingly as follows: “Though negligible differences in EC 50 or Emax from G-protein signaling, the dimer-reduced form (F1013.24A) showed a higher Emax than the dimeric form in the β-arrestin signaling (Supplementary Fig. 1f), consistent with previous results, which may be indicative that the dimer exhibits G-protein bias compared to the monomer.” 11. The apparent unity hill-slope of both cAMP and β-arrestin responses has no detectable change between the WT receptor and the F101A mutant (proposed monomeric form), nor does there appear to be a detectable change in pEC50. This suggests that in the dimeric form of the apelin receptor, there is no detectable co-operativity (negative or positive) for either ligand. Thermodynamically, it is hard to envision how dimerization would NOT alter ligand binding (see REF 6 and Birdsall, N.J.M. (2010). Class A GPCR heterodimers: evidence from binding studies. Trends Pharmacol. Sci. 31, 499–508. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tips.2010.08.003.). A statement to this effect should be included immediately after the above sentence: “No detectable change in either Hill-slope or pEC50 is evident for either AMG986 or JN241-9 between WT and monomeric (F101A) receptors, suggesting that ligand binding allostery, if present, is not detectable.” Response: We thank you for your valuable perspective. We have revised the description in our manuscript as follows: “Though negligible differences in EC or Emax from G- 50 protein signaling, the dimer-reduced form (F1013.24A) showed a higher Emax than the dimeric form in the β-arrestin signaling (Supplementary Fig. 1f), consistent with previous results1, which may be indicative that the dimer exhibits G-protein bias compared to the monomer. No detectable change in either Hill-slope or pEC is 50 evident for either AMG986 or JN241-9 between dimers (WT) and the dimer-reduced form (F1013.24A), suggesting that ligand binding allostery, if present, is not detectable.” 12. Page 5 lines 110-112. “Moreover, cAMP accumulation results showed that the dimer-reduced form exhibits higher constitutive activity than that of dimeric form (Supplementary Figs. 1d-e).” Please refer to the magnitude of change and also provide analysis supporting a statistically significant difference. I would also suggest softening this statement, as without data showing that receptor expression is equivalent AND that the WT v’s F101A mutant do not alter (for example) adenylate cyclase or phosphodiesterase expression it is not possible to attribute the change in baseline to receptor constitutive activity. A solution would be to perform assays using an inverse agonist for Apelin receptor, although I am not aware of one. I would suggest the following: “Moreover, cAMP accumulation results showed that the dimer-reduced form appear to exhibit ~25% higher constitutive activity than that of dimeric form (Supplementary Figs. 1d-e, p<0.ABC).” Response: We thank you for your valuable comments We have revised the description in our manuscript as follows: “Moreover, cAMP accumulation results showed that the dimer-reduced form appear to exhibit ~25% higher constitutive activity than that of dimeric form (Supplementary Figs. 1d-e, p < 0.001).” The curve for used for these concentration-response curves is not stated, either in the results or in the methods. Please include the equation used in the methods section. If a 3 parameter logistic equation has been used, this should be justified as it would fail to take into account 2:2 stoichiometry. Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this omission. The following sentence has been added to the Methods section: “Concentration-response curves were fitted using the ‘log (agonist) vs. response (Three parameters)’ model in GraphPad Prism 8 to obtain EC₅₀ values.” In addition, the three-parameter logistic model was selected as it is a standard and reliable statistical method for characterizing agonist efficacy and obtaining EC₅₀ values in GPCR signaling assays. 13. Page 5, line 120-122. “Here, we successfully achieved high-resolution cryo-EM structures of agonists-bound class A GPCR in various conformations without G-protein, delineating the dynamic process of activation.” Again, these are snapshots and there is no data that addresses whether they are all on the reaction pathway and if they are which order they occur. I suggest a more conservative interpretation of this data: “Here, we successfully achieved high-resolution cryo-EM structures of agonists-bound class A GPCR in various conformations without G-protein, providing potential insights into the dynamic process of activation.” Response: We thank you for your valuable suggestion. We have revised the description in our manuscript as follows: “Here, we successfully achieved high-resolution cryo-EM structures of agonists-bound class A GPCR in various conformations without G-protein, providing potential insights into the dynamic process of activation.” 14. Page 5, line 127. “Fortunately, we identified ….” Fortunately is unnecessary and pejorative, I suggest to start the sentence “We identified …..” Response: We thank you for your helpful comments. We have removed this unnecessary word in the manuscript accordingly. 15. Page 5, lines 133-135. “Additionally, the two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein are distinguished by unique conformational changes of TM6 and helix 8 (H8) in one protomer (termed by LBS2a and LBS2b, respectively) (Supplementary Fig. 2b).” Conformation changes are assumed not measured, these are snapshots and there is no reason to believe they represent a particular reaction co-ordinate. I suggest: “Additionally, the two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein are distinguished by unique conformations of TM6 and helix 8 (H8) in one protomer (termed by LBS2a and LBS2b, respectively) (Supplementary Fig. 2b).” Response: We thank you for your thoughtful comments. We have revised the description in our manuscript as follows: “Additionally, the two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein are distinguished by unique conformations of TM6 and helix 8 (H8) in one protomer (termed by LBS2a and LBS2b, respectively) (Supplementary Fig. 2b).” 16. Page 6, lines 136-137. “These results indicate that the conformations are in a ligand-dependent manner.” This sentence doesn’t make sense in English, I suggest: “These results indicate that the different ligands may select different conformational states.” Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this issue. We have revised the description in our manuscript as follows: “These results indicate that the different ligands may induce different conformational states.” 17. Page 6, lines 143-146. “Data processing revealed that AMG986-bound dimeric APLNR–Gi1 complexes adopt two conformations in protB (termed by ACT2a and ACT2b, respectively), aligning with those structures without G-protein (Supplementary Fig. 3b).” is there meant to be an alignment between G-protein free and G-protein bound complexes in Supp Fig 3b? I don’t see one? Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this careful observation. The original statement was indeed unclear. Supplementary Fig. 3b illustrates the two conformations (ACT2a and ACT2b) of the AMG986-bound dimeric APLNR–G complexes in protB, while i1 the corresponding two conformations (LBS2a and LBS2b) for the G-protein-free complexes are shown in Supplementary Fig. 2b. To prevent any misunderstanding, we have revised the description in the manuscript as follows: “Data processing revealed that AMG986-bound dimeric APLNR–G complexes adopt two conformations in i1 protB (termed by ACT2a and ACT2b, respectively), aligning with those structures without G-protein (Supplementary Figs. 2b and 3b).” 18. Page 6, lines 149-151. “To elucidate the structural transition of APLNR from its apo to active state, we first compared two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein (LBS2a and LBS2b) against the apo state to identify structural differences (Fig.2a)”. Implicit in this analysis is the assumption that the reaction co-ordinate for a GPCR to lower the energy barrier for nucleotide exchange at its cognate G protein involves binding of the agonist prior to binding of the G protein. What is the evidence that this is the case for the Apelin Receptor? The majority of Class A GPCRs where agonist binding has been studied such that G protein-coupling can be modulated by the addition of non-hydrolysable GTP analogues show that the high affinity state is one in which the G protein is engaged with the receptor. There are a range of Class A receptors where there is evidence of pre-coupling of G protein to receptor. Implicit in the ternary complex model is that G protein coupling may occur prior to agonist binding. Where is has been studied, apo GPCRs explore conformations that are either intermediate to activation or similar to fully active (ternary) conformations. Lastly, large scale MD simulations of many Class A GPCRs (including the Apelin receptor) supports the notion that these receptors explore active-like states in the absence of agonist binding. Taken together, and in the absence of data that supports agonist binding first, I think it is faulty logic to ascribe the agonist bound, G protein free state as a transition to the active state. It could be this, but it could also be a state that is not on the reaction pathway. Seed references are below: 1. Aranda-García, D., Stepniewski, T.M., Torrens-Fontanals, M. et al. Large scale investigation of GPCR molecular dynamics data uncovers allosteric sites and lateral gateways. Nat Commun 16, 2020 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57034-y 2. Kim TH, Chung KY, Manglik A, Hansen AL, Dror RO, Mildorf TJ, Shaw DE, Kobilka BK, Prosser RS. The role of ligands on the equilibria between functional states of a G protein-coupled receptor. J Am Chem Soc. 2013 Jun 26;135(25):9465-74. doi: 10.1021/ja404305k. Epub 2013 Jun 14. PMID: 23721409; PMCID: PMC3763947. 3. Nobles M, Benians A, Tinker A. Heterotrimeric G proteins precouple with G protein-coupled receptors in living cells. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2005 Dec 20;102(51):18706-11. doi: 10.1073/pnas.0504778102. Epub 2005 Dec 13. PMID: 16352729; PMCID: PMC1317907. 4. De Lean A, Stadel JM, Lefkowitz RJ. A ternary complex model explains the agonist-specific binding properties of the adenylate cyclase-coupled beta-adrenergic receptor. J Biol Chem. 1980 Aug 10;255(15):7108-17. PMID: 6248546. Following the professional opinion, we change our statement to “We first compared two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein (LBS2a and LBS2b) against the apo state to identify structural differences (Fig.2a)”. 19. Figure 2 and supplementary figure 4. There are a number of relatively subtle changes in side chain position/rotation that are ascribed as being part of the activation pathway. The apparent resolution of the relevant parts of the receptor appears to be between 2 and 2.2A (supp fig 2 and 3), which should allow good confidence in assigning these. The maps on which these models are based and the models themselves are not provided (or perhaps I can’t find them?), so it is not possible as a reviewer to independently verify the side-chain movements being presented. I could not find an editorial policy on making these data (maps and models) available to reviewers, but this would be best-practice. Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. The cryo-EM density maps and atomic models for all structures reported in this study have now been uploaded as supplementary files and are available for review. We hope this allows for a full and independent assessment of the side-chain conformations described. 20. Page 7, line 178. “Surprisingly, we observed ….”. No need for the pejorative surprising. Present the data and let the reader judge whether it is “surprising”. Response: We thank you for your helpful comments. We have removed this unnecessary word in the manuscript accordingly. 21. Page 7/8 lines 194-197. “These findings indicate that AMG986 can independently induce activation of a single protomer within the APLNR dimer, in contrast to JN241-9, which necessitates G-protein engagement for receptor activation.” These are snapshots of dynamic complexes and it is not clear that induced fit is in operation, I would encourage more cautious interpretation. I also note that if the authors interpretation is correct, one would predict that AMG986 would possess higher efficacy compared with JN241-9. I see no evidence of this. If this data quantitively and statistically supports faster cAMP inhibition kinetics if could be interpreted that the F101A mutant has higher propensity to pre-couple to its cognate G protein, thus increasing the agonist on-rate and subsequent Gi/o activation. Page 9, line 244. “Intriguingly, the ….” Please remove “intriguingly”. Response: We thank you for your helpful comments. We have removed this unnecessary word in the manuscript accordingly. 25. First based on the cryo-EM structures, the activation of a single protomer in the dimer is only induced by AMG986 leading to greater extent of dimer dissociation. Figure 4c. As a minimum, the authors need to provide parallel experiments where the effect of cholesterol depletion on basal adenylate cyclase activity is assesses in cells that do not express the apelin receptor. reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: I thank the authors for taking on board most of my comments and amending their manuscript accordingly. I am please that the authors performed the cholesterol depletion experiment on cells lacking the Apelin receptor (supp fig 8). Their conclusion, however, that the slightly smaller magnitude difference in basal cAMP for Aplein receptor containing cells v's control cells and between cholesterol replete and cholesterol depleted conditions (compared with a >2 fold effect of cholesterol depletion by itself) supports a role for cholesterol in Apelin signalling is, in my opinion, over-reach. Some data interpretation remains careless and unsystematic, including poor use of statistics, however I leave it in the editors hands to decide how this will be handled.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_5: The authors did a good job on revising the manuscript and most importantly showed the effect of cholesterol depletion on cAMP levels without the influence of receptors. Whereas I appreciate this additional information, I'm not supporting the way how the authors deal with this important additional results: The authors show the effect of cholesterol depletion on cAMP with and without Apelin receptors (Suppl. Figure 8d), where they see a reduction of cAMP levels to values of 38% without receptors. With expression of the receptors the decrease is enhanced to 30%. Even though this difference in 38% versus 30 % was significant, the wording in the text: "We found that depletion of cholesterol led to a decrease in the value of cAMP accumulation without affecting the expression of receptors (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 8b). This decrease reflects an enhancement in basal activity, indicating that the cholesterol depletion promotes the dissociation of dimers into monomers." is misleading as it suggests that the major decrease in cAMP is due to increase in the constitutive APLNR activity, which is not the case, as cholesterol depletion causes a major decrease cAMP even in cells not expressing the receptor (reduction to 38 % of initial values). The authors need to rephrase it in a way that misinterpretation is avoided. The data of Fig 4c need to be shown together with those of supplemental Figure 8d in order to be meaningful. Looking carefully at the data, which show that the cAMP Signal most likely due to stronger amplification is quite a bit more sensitive to apelin receptor activation compared to the Gi protein dissociation assay, I can clearly see why this assay is well suited to detect constitutive receptor activity. However, I’m puzzled that given the higher amplification, why it does not level out equally at high agonist concentrations, whereas the Gi protein assay does. This is important, because mutations in the apelin receptor that reduce cholesterol binding induce a shift of the cAMP signals over the whole range of agonist concentrations (Figure 4d), which would indicate that the mutation would not only increase the constitutive activity of the apelin receptor but also the maximal agonist efficacy. This is something that I would not expect to see in the more sensitive cAMP glow-sensor assay but rather in the Gi dissociation assay (less amplification and overexpressed G proteins). What do the authors think about this and how do they explain and discuss this issue in their manuscript. specific newly identified issue: The legend of Y axis of Supplemetary Figurte 1 a-c in my opinion is wrong or at least misleading: It should be assoziation and not dissoziation as with high agonits they will see an increase in G protein dissoziation and not a decrease. Otherwise the axis needs to be inverted.

peer_review_rounds.author_response: We thank the referees for their valuable time in reviewing our manuscript and the constructive suggestions that they have provided. We have carefully taken these comments into consideration in preparing a revised version of our manuscript. Please find below a point-by-point response to the referees with our responses in blue and the reviewers’ comments in black. Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author): I thank the authors for taking on board most of my comments and amending their manuscript accordingly. I am please that the authors performed the cholesterol depletion experiment on cells lacking the Apelin receptor (supp fig 8). Their conclusion, however, that the slightly smaller magnitude difference in basal cAMP for Aplein receptor containing cells v's control cells and between cholesterol replete and cholesterol depleted conditions (compared with a >2 fold effect of cholesterol depletion by itself) supports a role for cholesterol in Apelin signalling is, in my opinion, over-reach. Some data interpretation remains careless and unsystematic, including poor use of statistics, however I leave it in the editors hands to decide how this will be handled. Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s careful evaluation and valuable comments. We agree with the reviewer’s point that the slightly smaller magnitude difference in basal cAMP between APLNR-expressing and control cells under cholesterol-depleted conditions, compared to the substantial effect of cholesterol depletion itself, should be interpreted with more caution. As shown in our Supplementary Figure 8d, cholesterol depletion led to a pronounced 70% reduction in cAMP levels in APLNR-expressing cells, while a similarly strong reduction (62%) was observed in non-transfected control cells. This indicates that the effect of cholesterol depletion on cAMP is not solely attributable to enhanced basal activity of APLNR. In response to the reviewer’s comment, we have revised the corresponding statement in the manuscript to reflect a more tempered interpretation. The original description: “This decrease reflects an enhancement in basal activity, indicating that the cholesterol depletion promotes the dissociation of dimers into monomers.” has been modified to: “This decrease suggests a possible enhancement in basal activity, which would further suggest that the cholesterol depletion may promote the dissociation of dimers into monomers.” Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author): I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
