## Methods

Constructs

To prepare the cryo-EM sample of AMG986- and JN241-9-bound APLNR without G-protein, human wild type full-length APLNR (UniProt: P35414) was cloned into pFastBac1 vector (Invitrogen) with an N-terminal hemagglutinin (HA) signal sequence connected to a Flag tag. To further improve APLNR expression, a thermostabilized BRIL was fused to the N-terminus after the Flag-tag. A double MBP tag followed by a C-terminal His tag was fused into the C terminal of APLNR with a linker containing a TEV protease cleavage site. Unlike the construct for JN241-9-bound APLNR, LgBit was added at the end of TEV protease site in the construct of AMG986-bound APLNR. To prepare the cryo-EM sample of AMG986- and JN241-9-bound APLNR–Gi1 complexes, an N-terminal HA signal sequence connected to a Flag-tag was fused to the N-terminal APLNR. Human dominant-negative (DN) Gαi1 was generated by site-directed mutagenesis to decrease the nucleotide-binding affinity and increase the stability of G-protein60. Human Gβ1 was cloned into pFastBac dual vector with Gγ2. In addition, the scFv16, which encodes the single-chain variable fragment of mAb16, was subcloned into pFastBac plasmid.

To analyze G-protein signaling through NanoBit assay and cAMP accumulation assay, a Flag-tag was fused to the N-terminal of full-length and various mutants of APLNR. Additionally, Gαi1 was fused with LgBit, and Gγ was fused with SmBiT, and all three constructs were cloned into pcDNA3.1 plasmids. For β-arrestin signaling analysis, the C-terminus of the APLNR receptor was fused with the Rluc8 fragment, the Venus fragment was inserted into the N-terminus of β-arrestin2 and then both were cloned into pBiT1.1 plasmids (Promega).

Expression and purification of scFv16

The secreted scFv16 protein was expressed and purified using the bac-to-bac system. Briefly, the scFv16 with a C-terminal histidine-tag was overexpressed in Trichoplusia ni Hi5 insect cells for 48 h and purified by Ni-NTA resin. The eluted protein was cleaved by 3C protease and further purified by gel filtration chromatography using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare). The purified scFv16 fractions were concentrated and stored at -80 °C until use.

Expression and purification of JN241-9

JN241-9 with a 6× His tag at the C-terminal was expressed in the periplasm of E. coli BL21 cells. Briefly, JN241-9 target gene was transformed in the bacterium and amplified in TB culture medium. When OD600 reached 0.7-1.2, 1 mM IPTG was added to induce expression followed by overnight incubation at 28 °C. JN241-9 was purified by Ni-NTA resin. The eluted protein was collected and then desalted using a HiPrep 26/10 Desalting column. Fractions of JN241-9 were concentrated to ~8 mg/ml and quickly frozen in the liquid nitrogen with 10% glycerol and stored at −80 °C.

Expression and purification of agonists-APLNR

APLNR constructs were expressed in sf9 insect cells using the bac-to-bac Baculovirus Expression System (Invitrogen). The cells were then incubated for 48 h at 27 °C and subsequently collected by centrifugation at 1,000 × g for 30 min. Cell precipitates were stored at -80 °C until further use. The cell pellets were suspended in buffer containing 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 2 mM MgCl2, 100 mM NaCl, protease inhibitor cocktail (Bimake) and agonist (100 nM AMG986 or 1 μM JN241-9). The membranes were solubilized with 0.5% (w/v) lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) and 0.1% (w/v) cholesterol hemisuccinate (CHS) for 2 h at 4 °C and separated by centrifugation at 30,000g for 30 min. Following incubation with amylose resin (NEB), and the protein was eluted with 20 mM maltose. TEV protease was then added for 1 h to remove the 2×MBP protein. After concentrated, the protein was loaded onto Superose 6 Increase 10/ 300 GL (GE Healthcare) column with running buffer containing 20 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 0.00075% (w/v) LMNG, 0.00025% (w/v) glyco-diosgenin (GDN), 0.0002% (w/v) CHS and agonist (100 nM AMG986 or 1 μM JN241-9). The monomeric peak fractions were collected and concentrated to 10-15 mg/ml for electron microscopy experiments.

Expression and purification of agonists–APLNR–Gi1 Complexes

APLNR, Gαi1 and Gβγ constructs were co-expressed at the ratio of 1:1:1 in sf9 insect cells using the bac-to-bac Baculovirus Expression System (Invitrogen). The cells were then incubated for 48 h at 27 °C and subsequently collected by centrifugation at 1,000 × g for 30 min. For the purification of APLNR–Gi1 complexes, the cell pellets were suspended in buffer containing 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 2 mM MgCl2, 100 mM NaCl and protease inhibitor cocktail (Bimake), followed by addition of 1.2 mg scFv16 antibody, 12 mU/ml apyrase (Sigma), and agonist (100 nM AMG986 or 1 μM JN241-9). The mixture was incubated for 1 h at room temperature for complex formation. After that, the membranes were solubilized with 0.5% (w/v) LMNG and 0.1% (w/v) CHS for 2 h at 4 °C. The supernatant was then separated by centrifugation at 30,000g for 30 min. Following incubation with anti-FLAG affinity resin, the protein was eluted with 0.2 mg/ml Flag peptide. Add 10% (w/w) scFv16 antibody and incubated for 15 min at room temperature. The elution was concentrated with a 100 kDa cut-off concentrator (Millipore) and loaded onto a Superose 6 increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare) with a running buffer containing 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 0.00075% LMNG, 0.0002% (w/v) CHS, 0.00025% (w/v) GDN and agonist (100 nM AMG986 or 1 μM JN241-9). The monomeric peak fractions were collected and concentrated to 10-15 mg/ml for electron microscopy experiments.

Cryo-EM grid preparation and data collection

To prepare cryo-EM grids, purified complexes (3 μL, ~10 mg/ml) were applied individually to the grids that were subsequently flash frozen in liquid ethane using Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific) under 100% humidity at 4 C. For AMG986-, JN241-9-bound APLNR and AMG986-, JN241-9-bound APLNR–Gi1 complexes, cryo-EM data collection was performed on a Titan Krios at 300 kV accelerating voltage. Micrographs were recorded using a Falcon 4 direct electron detector in super-resolution mode with a pixel size of 0.93 Å using EPU software. Image stacks were obtained at a dose rate of about 13.24 electrons per Å2 per second with a defocus ranging from -1.0 to -2.5 μm. The total exposure time was 3.92 s, and 40 frames were recorded per micrograph.

Cryo-EM data processing

Dose-fractionated image stacks were aligned using MotionCor2.161, implemented in Relion 4.0. Contrast transfer function (CTF) parameters for each micrograph were estimated by Gctf v1.1862. The following data processing was performed using RELION 4.0 and CryoSPARC v4.0.363,64.

For the JN241-9-bound APLNR complex, a total of 13,193,854 particles were auto-picked in Relion 4.0. High-quality particle projections from multiple rounds of 2D classification and Heterogenous Refinement were utilized for ab-initio reconstruction to generate initial reference maps. A good subset of 2,817,890 particle projections was subjected to Heterogenous Refinement and 2D classification and two distinct particle populations were discerned, corresponding to the APLNR monomer and APLNR dimer. A subsequent round of 3D classification for APLNR dimer yielded three particle subsets: JN241-9-dimerLBS1a, JN241-9–dimerLBS1b and JN241-9–dimerLBS1c. These subsets of 97,020 particles, 101,362 particles and 138,605 particles were subjected to 3D refinement, CTF refinement, and Bayesian polishing in Relion, generating three maps with a global resolution of 2.7 Å.

For the AMG986-bound APLNR complex, a total of 14,104,471 particles were auto-picked. Particles from multiple rounds of 2D classification and Heterogenous Refinement were utilized for ab-initio reconstruction to generate initial reference maps. A good subset of 2,271,602 particle projections was subjected to Heterogenous Refinement and 2D classification, identifying APLNR monomer and APLNR dimer populations. Further 3D classification yielded two particle subsets: AMG-dimerLBS2a and AMG-dimerLBS2b. These subsets of 306,883 particles and 288,225 particles were subjected to 3D refinement, CTF refinement, and Bayesian polishing in Relion, generating two maps with a global resolution of 2.4 Å for AMG–dimerLBS2a and 2.5 Å for AMG–dimerLBS2b.

For the JN241-9-bound APLNR–Gi1 complex, a total of 16,153,222 particles were auto-picked. Particles from multiple rounds of 2D classification and Heterogenous Refinement were utilized for ab-initio reconstruction to generate initial reference maps. 4,170,567 particles were subjected to Heterogenous Refinement and 2D classification and four distinct particle populations were discerned: JN241-9–monomer, JN241-9–dimer JN241-9–monomer–Gi and JN241-9–dimer–Gi. A subsequent round of 3D classification for JN241-9–dimer also yielded three particle subsets: LBS1a, LBS1b and LBS1c. Final subsets of 187,827 particles for JN241-9–monomer–Gi and 198,168 particles for JN241-9–dimer–Gi were subjected to 3D refinement, CTF refinement, and Bayesian polishing in Relion, generating two maps with a global resolution of 2.5 Å and 3.0 Å, respectively.

For the AMG986-bound APLNR–Gi1 complex, a total of 6,477,441 particles were auto-picked. Particles from 2D classification and Heterogenous Refinement were utilized for ab-initio reconstruction to generate initial reference maps. A good subset of 1,257,292 particle projections was subjected to Heterogenous Refinement and 2D classification and four populations were discerned: AMG986–monomer, AMG986–dimer AMG986–monomer–Gi and AMG986–dimer–Gi. The final subset of 63,229 particles for AMG986–monomer–Gi were subjected to 3D refinement, CTF refinement, and Bayesian polishing in Relion, generating a map with a global resolution of 2.8 Å.

Comprehensive refinement metrics are detailed in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

Model building and refinement

The model of Apelin receptor in complex with single-domain antibody (PDB: 6KNM) was used to generate the initial template of receptor30. The atomic coordinates of Gi and scFv16 from the structure of MM07-bound APLNR–Gi1 complex (PDB: 8XZH) were used to generate the initial template of the G-protein complex19. Models were docked into the cryo-EM density map using UCSF Chimera65. Agonist coordinates and geometry restraints were generated using a phenix.elbow66. The docked model was subjected to flexible fitting using Rosetta 2019.35 and iterative manual adjustment in Coot and real-space-refined in Phenix67. The final refinement statistics were validated using the module ‘comprehensive validation (cryo-EM)’ in Phenix66. The goodness-of-fit of the model to the map was determined using a global model-versus-map Fourier shell correlation. The refinement statistics are provided in supplementary information. Structural figures were created using UCSF Chimera and the UCSF Chimera X package65,68.

NanoBiT-G-protein dissociation assay

G-protein activation was measured using a NanoBiT G-protein dissociation assay.2 HEK293T cells were seeded in a 6-well plate and plasmid transfection was performed with a mixture of 600 ng Gαi, 500 ng Sm-Gβ, 500 ng Gγ2, 200 ng APLNR plasmid (per well). After 6 h of transfection, cells were digested and resuspended in complete DMEM medium (5% FBS, 1% antibiotic) and plated in 96-well flat-bottomed white microplates at a volume of 100 μl per well. Next day, the cells were washed twice with D-PBS and incubated in 40 μl of 5 μM coelenterazine A solution diluted with HBSS (assay buffer) for 40 min at room temperature. After baseline luminescence was measured for 3 cycles (Tecan), test ligands (5×, diluted in the HBSS assay buffer) were added to the cells (10 μl per well) and incubated for 3-5 min at room temperature before the second measurement was taken. The ligand-induced signal ratio was normalized to the baseline luminescence, and fold-change signals over vehicle treatment were used to show the G-protein dissociation response. Concentration-response curves were fitted using the “log (agonist) vs. response (Three parameters)” model in GraphPad Prism 8 to obtain EC₅₀ values.

cAMP accumulation assay

Human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK293T) cells were seeded in a 6-well plate and transfected with a plasmid mixture consisting of 1,500 ng receptor and 500 ng cAMP biosensor GloSensor-22F (Promega). After 6 h, transfected cells were plated onto a 96-well plate. After another 12 h, cells were washed twice with D-PBS and then incubated in CO2-independent media (assay buffer) containing 2% GloSensor cAMP Reagent (Promega) and 1 μM Forskolin at a volume of 40 μl per well. MβCD with various concentrations was added to assay buffer when investigating the stabilized effect of cholesterols. The transfected cells were incubated for 30 min in 37 °C CO2 incubator and another 30 min at room temperature in the dark before measurements for baseline luminescence (Spark Multimode microplate reader, TECAN). Next, test ligands (5×, diluted in CO2-independent media containing 1 μM Forskolin) were added to the cells (10 μl per well) and incubated for 15-20 min at room temperature before the second measurement was taken. Concentration-response curves were fitted using the “log (agonist) vs. response (Three parameters)” model in GraphPad Prism 8 to obtain EC₅₀ values.

Bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) assay

BRET assay was used to detect β-arrestin recruitment. HEK293T cells were transiently co-transfected with APLNR-Rluc8 and Venus-β-arrestin2 (1:4). The transfected cells were seeded into 96-well flat-bottomed white microplates at a volume of 100 μl per well. After 24 h, cells were washed twice with D-PBS and then maintained in the BRET buffer (containing 10 mM HEPES and 0.1% BSA) at a volume of 45 ml per well for 30 min in 37 °C CO2 incubator. Luciferase substrate coelenterazine h (5 μM) was then added to the transfected cells. Coelenterazine and cells were incubated together in the dark for 10 min and the plate was placed into the microplate reader to read the base value. Transfected cells were then stimulated with ligands (5 μl) at different concentrations and read with the microplate reader again to get the BRET signal value. Both the BRET signal value and the base value were determined as the ratio of light emitted by Venus-tagged biosensors and light emitted by Rluc8-tagged biosensors. The BRET acceptor (520-560 nm) and BRET donor (460-485 nm) emission signals were measured using the Spark Multimode microplate reader (Tecan). Venus’s fluorescence was measured before reading luminescence and calculated as average fluorescence from each control well. The BRET signal from the same well was determined as the ratio of the light emitted by Venus (520-560 nm) over that emitted by RLuc8 (460-485 nm). Concentration-response curves were fitted using the “log (agonist) vs. response (Three parameters)” model in GraphPad Prism 8 to obtain EC₅₀ values.

Cell-surface ELISA

Membrane expression of APLNR was determined by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to detect the N-terminal Flag tag on the WT and mutants transiently expressed in HEK293T cells. After transfection, cells were seeded into 96-well flat-bottomed white microplates at a volume of 100 μl per well. After 24 h, cells were washed twice with PBS and fixed with 4% formaldehyde for 10 min followed by three times washing with PBS. Then cells were incubated with blocking buffer (1% BSA in PBS) for 1 h at room temperature. Afterwards, cells were incubated with anti-FLAG M2 HRP-conjugated monoclonal antibody (Sigma Aldrich) in blocking buffer for 30 min at room temperature. After washing three times with PBS, 80 μl/well diluent SuperSignal Elisa Femto Maximum Sensitivity Substrate (ThermoFisher Scientific) was added. Luminance signal was measured at 1-s intervals for 500 ms/per well.

An analysis of 234 structures from 45 class A GPCRs in previous studies revealed a common activation mechanism that integrates key motifs (CWxP, PIF, Na⁺ pocket, NPxxY and DRY) into a unified conformational pathway2. This pathway operates through four hierarchical layers (Fig. R13): Layer 1: Signal Initiation. Agonist binding disrupts Na⁺-coordinated residues (D2.50, S3.39, N7.45), triggering inward movement of TM7, and residues at TM3 (3.40) and TM6 (6.44, 6.48) repack, initiating outward movement of TM6’s cytoplasmic end. Layer 2: Hydrophobic Lock Opening. Breaking of hydrophobic contacts (PIF motif) between TM3, TM5 and TM6, releasing TM6. Meanwhile, W6.48 rotation destabilizes TM6, facilitating its outward shift. Layer 3: Microswitch Rewiring. Y7.53 loses contacts with TM1/helix 8 and forms new bonds with TM3 (R3.50, I3.46), strengthening TM3-TM7 coupling. TM7 inward movement further displaces TM6 (NPxxY motif). Layer 4: G-Protein Coupling. Ionic lock (DRY motif) breaks, releasing R3.50. This residue engages Gα, while TM6’s outward shift creates a G-protein binding cavity. In summary, activation of GPCRs involves a conserved conformational rearrangement of key motifs, resulting in the outward displacement of TM6. Concurrently, TM7 moves inward to stabilize the active conformation of TM6. The NPxxY motif, situated at the intracellular end of TM7, exhibits the largest structural transition from the apo to the active state among all conserved motifs. Reply figure 13. Common activation pathway of class A GPCRs2. Homo dimers are reported to form for lots of class A receptors and B receptors, can they authors comment how common their findings might be? Response: Thank you for your comments. While class C GPCRs are known to mediate signaling only in a dimeric form, class A and class B GPCRs were initially believed to function exclusively as monomers. However, evidence supporting dimerization in class A and class B receptors emerged with the development of advanced techniques such as photoaffinity labeling and cross-linking, which identified homodimers of β -adrenergic 2 receptor and heterodimers between cholecystokinin-8 (CCK-8) and dopamine (DA) receptors3,4. The existence of GPCR dimers is now well supported by a range of biochemical approaches, including epitope-tagging, immunoprecipitation, FRET and BRET assays. In class A GPCRs, several homodimer forms have been validated through these approaches: β₂-adrenergic receptor (β₂-AR), somatostatin receptor 5 (SSTR5), and δ-/κ-opioid receptors5; AT1R and A₂AR6; CCR2 and CCR57; apelin receptor8, and M₃ muscarinic receptor (M₃R)9. In addition, functionally relevant heterodimers have also been reported, such as the dopamine D₁ receptor and adenosine A₁ receptor complex10. Class B GPCRs also exhibit dimerization and oligomerization properties. GLP-1R has been confirmed to form homodimers through multiple resonance energy transfer assays, with TM4 identified as the interface of the dimeric interaction11. ECD-mediated oligomerization of PTH1R was similarly confirmed in living cells using BRET and FRET techniques12. Additionally, the GIPR has been shown to suppress PAC1 receptor-driven neuronal differentiation through heterocomplex formation13. Powerful advances in single-molecule microscopy have facilitated the measurements of the dynamic process of GPCR dimerization in real time. Homodimerization has been frequently reported for several class A GPCRs using various techniques: spot intensity analysis (APLNR, β AR, β AR, M R, FPR, D R)8,14- 1 2 1 3 17; photobleach step counting (μOR, PAFR, M R)18-20, and two-color coincidence 2 detection (S1P3R, mCannR2)21,22. These studies indicate that the dimeric formation of the receptor is transient and density-dependent. TIRFM is particularly suitable for assessing these dynamic membrane processes and quantifying oligomeric states. For example, at densities below 0.3 receptor particles/μm², ~60% of APLNR and ~44% of PAFR molecules formed dimers or oligomers. In class B GPCRs, CRF1R has shown a stable monomer/dimer equilibrium both at the plasma membrane and in the ER, as revealed by TIRFM23. The frequency and relevance of GPCR dimerization in vivo remains under debate. Some findings are derived from receptor overexpression systems, which may introduce experimental artifacts. Advanced imaging tools, such as super-resolution microscopy, can further surpasses the diffraction limit, offering quantitative insights into the stoichiometry of receptor oligomers. Given the limited structural understanding of class A and class B GPCR dimers, our study provides additional evidence supporting the existence of APLNR homodimer and elucidates a dynamic monomer–dimer transition mechanism that contributes to a deeper understanding of complex downstream signaling. ### Reviewer 1

Authors have clearly resolved all of my concerns in the revised manuscript. However, I strongly suggest that authors should add references to the revised line 272~288 (that correspond to Q#2) to provide clarity to the readers.

### Reviewer 3

I have been asked to review this manuscript after preliminary revision due to the withdrawal of review #2. The manuscript by Ji et al. describes twelve cryo-EM assemblies in detergent micelles of engineered apelin receptor with two different (non-physiological) agonists (AMG986 and JN241-9) with and without engineered Galphai/Beta1/gamma2 heterotrimer. The authors then use these twelve assemblies to construct a narrative on possible conformational transitions for the apelin receptor during activation. They use the molecular snapshots provided by these cryo-EM assemblies to argue for a particular reaction pathway. There is no way to know whether the proposed relationship between the reported assemblies represents the pathway that occurs in their highly reconstituted and engineered system, much less in either a recombinant cellular setting or physiologically. The supporting cell-based assay data is heavily normalized (minimum 2 normalization steps), which hampers independent assessment by the reader, and in several cases lacks appropriate controls to allow interpretation. Throughout, the findings from their cryo-EM assemblies are referred to as if they represent some physiological ground truth, which is a serious, unsupported, over-interpretation. I urge the authors to apply a much more conservative interpretation of their data. I also note that the novelty of the manuscript is undermined by existing publications of apelin receptor structures reported elsewhere, including by these authors. I would strongly suggest that the term “aggregation”, which the authors appear to use to mean dimerization / oligomerization should be replaced with either of these terms. Aggregation has a specific meaning in biochemistry, which is: the accumulation of misfolded or intrinsically disordered proteins into (typically) insoluble, non-functional complexes. Understanding whether GPCRs (outside Class C) do form dimers in physiological settings, and if they do, what the functional consequence is, remains an unresolved question in the field. Unfortunately, the field is largely divided into dogmatic camps of “GPCR dimerization is a general phenomenon with important physiological outcomes” and “GPCR dimerization is an artefact, with no relevance at all”. Despite the large amount of literature on the subject, conclusions remain equivocal, due to a fairly large body of literature that relies on transfected cell studies using various proximity measures that are not powered to detect the difference between close proximity and protein:protein interaction AND the difficulty in performing definitive experiments in physiologically meaningful settings. There is no teleological reason to believe GPCRs form dimers, unlike nuclear hormone receptors (dimerization required for DNA binding), receptor tyrosine kinases (dimerization required for transphosphorylation) or enzymes (dimerization provides positive or negative allostery to enable physiologically relevant sensitivity to changes in substrate availability). On the other hand, it is attractive to think that novel behaviors could emerge through the formation of GPCR heterodimers (although there is much evidence, particularly from the 1990’s to suggest signal crosstalk as a mechanism for new behaviors). In this setting, new publications on either side of this debate ought to be subject to careful critical analysis. Introduction: Page 2, lines 37-40 “GPCRs serve as central hubs in cellular signal transduction, ensuring the complexity and precision of downstream signaling through their structural versatility, characterized by diverse aggregated forms and dynamic conformational changes.” This is a meaningless word-salad, adding nothing to the paper. I would recommend removing. Page 2, lines 41-42 “Class A GPCRs exist in a dynamic equilibrium between monomeric and oligomeric forms”. Of the data cited none provide evidence for a dynamic equilibria between oligomeric states, a single figure in reference 6 (figure 3) has data that supports the contention that oxytocin receptors may form dimers in native tissue. The remainder of the citations rely on data that have alternative interpretations. I am concerned that there is an uncritical perpetuation of data over-interpretation supported by poor-quality and often careless experiments. Here are alternative interpretations for the common experimental types presented in these figures: • Co-immunoprecipitation. With the inclusion of all relevant controls (particularly for membrane proteins that have a propensity to aggregate), co-immunoprecipitation should only be used to conclude that 2 proteins are present as part of a complex, direct interaction cannot be concluded. Absence of data from native tissue should be viewed with scepticism. Antibodies for GPCRs are frequently un-specific. • Confocal microscopy showing “co-localisation”. Under standard techniques in an optimally adjusted system with a high NA objective the point-spread-function of GFP/Alexa488 is ~140 nm in the x-y and 380 nm in the z with a volume of about 4 x 10^6 nm^3 (obviously this gets bigger with longer wavelength). A typical GPCR occupies a volume of about 70 nm^3 , thus over 50,000 GPCRs can fit into a single PSF. Data is frequently reported where GPCRs do not appear to be localized to the plasma membrane, which is inconsistent with known properties. Antibodies for GPCRs are frequently un-specific. • BRET or FRET (resonance energy transfer techniques). Generally, only applicable in transfected cell studies. Relies on the assumption that direct interaction is required for resonance energy transfer. This is clearly not true, given the widespread use of bystander BRET to measure (for example) GPCR trafficking. Saturation BRET remains problematic as controls are difficult. If partner proteins for both donor and acceptor traffic to the same membrane subdomains, the readout for this assay will appear to indicate a specific interaction. Unless controls for collisional (random) BRET signals have equivalent expression (on a per-cell basis) to the test AND have comparable trafficking, interpretation is ambiguous. • Altered signalling output in the presence of a second GPCR. This could equally occur due to signal crosstalk. • Mutational analysis of putative dimerization interface (mostly TM bundle mutations, typically altering signalling output). Even if carefully controlled for expression level it is usually not possible to exclude the possibility that the mutation alters transmission of ligand binding event through the GPCR to its intracellular partner. Page 3 ,lines 52-55 “….supported by single-molecule imaging that confirms dimeric formation, and it is the first Class A GPCR whose stable dimeric structures have been captured by cryo-EM^8,15,16.” Reference 8 is provided to the contention that apelin receptor can interchange between dimers and monomers in cells (including using single molecule imaging). This reference is problematic, clustering (single molecule experiments, figure 1) lack appropriate controls (e.g. monomeric cell-surface receptor). If taken at face value, there is no equivalence between clustering and dimerization, this is below the resolution of the experiment. Even if dimerization is accepted there is not necessarily and equivalence between physical co-localisation and functional dimerization. Figure 2a, heavily cropped and manipulated western blots, non-equivalent loading of “mix” control, full blots not provided in supplementary information. Panels 2b&c are much more problematic, Oxytocin receptor is used as a ‘negative’ control in BRET experiments (i.e. as a receptor that does not dimerise), this is despite the fact that Reference 5 specifically demonstrates oxytocin receptor dimers by both FRET (weak evidence) but also by ligand allostery on native membranes (strong evidence), dimerization of oxytocin receptor is also reported in PMID: 27420737. Figure 3 & 4, no negative OR positive controls with both donor and acceptor included. Figure 5 uses interference peptides to infer TM1,2,3 & 4 as parts of the dimerization interface, this conflicts with data from PMID 35817871 (e.g. 7W0L) where TM4 plays no part and TM2 has only a single residue within a distance that could support an interaction (also noting that this is consistent with the present publication) bringing into question this methodology. The remaining figures also lack appropriate controls. I would suggest rephrasing to more accurately reflect the ambiguity of data: “APLNR is a model system that may be suitable for investigating the dynamic transition between monomeric and dimeric forms of class A GPCR, supported by transfected cell studies, and cryo-EM^8,15,16.” The clinical trial and published data on AMG986/Azelaprag is presented in a way that the reader might think that biased agonism and/or dimeric/monomeric receptor signalling profile is the reason for the clinical trial discontinuation (page 3, lines 71-74): “However, a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating AMG986 was recently discontinued owing to potential adverse effects, highlighting the necessity to explore its molecular mechanism in stimulating various apelin receptor forms.” This does not seem to be the most parsimonious interpretation as the clinical trial was terminated due to ~5% of patients in the Azelaprag arm having blood markers consistent with liver toxicity (no patients in control arm). The size of the trial suggests that this is, in fact, an Azelaprag side effect, however the most likely cause is off-target liver toxicity, not an undesirable on-target effect, as implied by the authors. I suggest removing the second half of this sentence and replace with: ““However, a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating AMG986 was recently discontinued owing to potential off-target liver toxicity.” No observation of transitions between different conformations is made in this manuscript. This would require NMR, single molecule FRET or HDX-MS (if the transitions are slow enough), or MD-simulations could be conducted to model transitions. None of these are performed in this manuscript, only static snapshots are determined with no way of knowing whether these occur in a particular order on a reaction pathway OR whether some are off-pathway conformations. Page 4, lines 85-87: “We therefore directly observed the stepwise transition and conformational changes of APLNR dimers towards monomers from the apo to the active state.” I suggest rephrasing to: “We therefore directly observed a range of conformational states of APLNR dimers and monomers, both apo and active states, which provide potential pathways for conformational transition between these states.” Results: Page 4, line 96 “…. network formed by F101^3.24 plays a …..” Here I assume the 3.24 refers to the Ballesteros-Weinstein numbering system for TM helices of GPCRs, please explain this to the reader and include the appropriate reference. I suggest “…. network formed by F101^3.24 (where the superscript refers to the Ballesteros-Weinstein transmembrane numbering system (ref)) plays a …..”. Reference is: Ballesteros, J.A., and Weinstein, H. (1995). Integrated methods for the construction of three-dimensional models and computational probing of structure-function relations in G protein-coupled receptors. Methods Neurosci. 25, 366–428. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1043-9471(05)80049-7. Page 4, lines 102-104: “AMG986 showed roughly 10-fold greater potency in activating various G-proteins, including Gi, Gq and G13, as well as β-arrestin, compared to JN241-9.” Please provide statistical analysis to support this difference. The appropriate analysis is to derive the pEC50 from each biological repeat, use this to derive a mean and error then test for difference between pEC50s (one-way ANOVA). It is more appropriate to display SD rather than SEM, since the former is an estimate of the biological variance. I note that supplemental file “583494_1_related_ms_11086941_sz33ll” contains individual columns that appear to sum to the total of technical replicates multiplied by biological repeats. Could the authors please confirm that they have no conflated technical and biological replicates? While Nature Communications makes no formal recommendation on use of error bars (see: https://www.nature.com/collections/qghhqm and https://www.nature.com/articles/nmeth.2659), best practice for this type of data would be SD. I also note that the double normalisation (individual baseline normalization, followed by conversion to fold over baseline, followed by conversion to % of WT-AMG896 Emax) has the potential to obscure differences in G protein activation whilst also potentially accentuating differences between ligands. I would prefer to see data where the final normalization step is removed. Page 4/5, lines 105-106. “Additionally, AMG986 induced a more rapid activation rate than JN241-9 (Supplementary Fig. 1d).” Firstly, please comment on the magnitude of difference, looking at the data this is very small and is hard to envision why one would think this is of any biological relevance. Secondly, please provide analysis to support that this difference is statistically significant. Third, as with the above comment, I suggest SD. The axis of supp fig 1d is labelled “cAMP accumulation %”, this is the % of what? For all cAMP data, are the authors confident that sensor has not been saturated? For example, was a cell permeant cAMP analoge (e.g. 8-CPT) included at the end of the assay? Page 5, lines 107-108. “Though negligible differences in EC50 or Emax from G-protein signaling, the dimer-reduced form (F1013.24A) showed a higher Emax than the dimeric form in the β-arrestin signaling (Supplementary Fig. 1f).” Please refer to the magnitude of change and also provide analysis supporting a statistically significant difference. Without experiments performed under parallel conditions to quantitate cell-surface expression this change in Emax could be as a result of altered receptor number. Elsewhere (supp fig 8) the authors report cell surface expression by ELISA, however it is not clear from the methods that this was performed under equivalent transfection conditions to the β-arrestin assay. It is not clear from the methods whether cell integrity would be maintained using the fixation technique used and no negative control is included. As this data stands, interpretation is ambiguous. I suggest a cautious interpretation of this result: “Though negligible differences in EC50 or Emax from G-protein signaling, the dimer-reduced form (F1013.24A) showed a higher Emax than the dimeric form in the β-arrestin signaling (Supplementary Fig. 1f), consistent with previous results^15, which may be indicative that the dimer exhibits G-protein bias compared to the monomer.” The apparent unity hill-slope of both cAMP and β-arrestin responses has no detectable change between the WT receptor and the F101A mutant (proposed monomeric form), nor does there appear to be a detectable change in pEC50. This suggests that in the dimeric form of the apelin receptor, there is no detectable co-operativity (negative or positive) for either ligand. Thermodynamically, it is hard to envision how dimerization would NOT alter ligand binding (see REF 6 and Birdsall, N.J.M. (2010). Class A GPCR heterodimers: evidence from binding studies. Trends Pharmacol. Sci. 31, 499–508. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tips.2010.08.003.). A statement to this effect should be included immediately after the above sentence: “No detectable change in either Hill-slope or pEC50 is evident for either AMG986 or JN241-9 between WT and monomeric (F101A) receptors, suggesting that ligand binding allostery, if present, is not detectable.” Page 5 lines 110-112. “Moreover, cAMP accumulation results showed that the dimer-reduced form exhibits higher constitutive activity than that of dimeric form (Supplementary Figs. 1d-e).” Please refer to the magnitude of change and also provide analysis supporting a statistically significant difference. I would also suggest softening this statement, as without data showing that receptor expression is equivalent AND that the WT v’s F101A mutant do not alter (for example) adenylate cyclase or phosphodiesterase expression it is not possible to attribute the change in baseline to receptor constitutive activity. A solution would be to perform assays using an inverse agonist for Apelin receptor, although I am not aware of one. I would suggest the following: “Moreover, cAMP accumulation results showed that the dimer-reduced form appear to exhibit ~25% higher constitutive activity than that of dimeric form (Supplementary Figs. 1d-e, p<0.ABC).” The curve for used for these concentration-response curves is not stated, either in the results or in the methods. Please include the equation used in the methods section. If a 3 parameter logistic equation has been used, this should be justified as it would fail to take into account 2:2 stoichiometry. Page 5, line 120-122. “Here, we successfully achieved high-resolution cryo-EM structures of agonists-bound class A GPCR in various conformations without G-protein, delineating the dynamic process of activation.” Again, these are snapshots and there is no data that addresses whether they are all on the reaction pathway and if they are which order they occur. I suggest a more conservative interpretation of this data: “Here, we successfully achieved high-resolution cryo-EM structures of agonists-bound class A GPCR in various conformations without G-protein, providing potential insights into the dynamic process of activation.” Page 5, line 127. “Fortunately, we identified ….” Fortunately is unnecessary and pejorative, I suggest to start the sentence “We identified …..” Page 5, lines 133-135. “Additionally, the two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein are distinguished by unique conformational changes of TM6 and helix 8 (H8) in one protomer (termed by LBS2a and LBS2b, respectively) (Supplementary Fig. 2b).” Conformation changes are assumed not measured, these are snapshots and there is no reason to believe they represent a particular reaction co-ordinate. I suggest: “Additionally, the two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein are distinguished by unique conformations of TM6 and helix 8 (H8) in one protomer (termed by LBS2a and LBS2b, respectively) (Supplementary Fig. 2b).” Page 6, lines 136-137. “These results indicate that the conformations are in a ligand-dependent manner.” This sentence doesn’t make sense in English, I suggest: “These results indicate that the different ligands may select different conformational states.” Page 6, lines 143-146. “Data processing revealed that AMG986-bound dimeric APLNR–Gi1 complexes adopt two conformations in protB (termed by ACT2a and ACT2b, respectively), aligning with those structures without G-protein (Supplementary Fig. 3b).” is there meant to be an alignment between G-protein free and G-protein bound complexes in Supp Fig 3b? I don’t see one? Page 6, lines 149-151. “To elucidate the structural transition of APLNR from its apo to active state, we first compared two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein (LBS2a and LBS2b) against the apo state to identify structural differences (Fig.2a)”. Implicit in this analysis is the assumption that the reaction co-ordinate for a GPCR to lower the energy barrier for nucleotide exchange at its cognate G protein involves binding of the agonist prior to binding of the G protein. What is the evidence that this is the case for the Apelin Receptor? The majority of Class A GPCRs where agonist binding has been studied such that G protein-coupling can be modulated by the addition of non-hydrolysable GTP analogues show that the high affinity state is one in which the G protein is engaged with the receptor. There are a range of Class A receptors where there is evidence of pre-coupling of G protein to receptor. Implicit in the ternary complex model is that G protein coupling may occur prior to agonist binding. Where is has been studied, apo GPCRs explore conformations that are either intermediate to activation or similar to fully active (ternary) conformations. Lastly, large scale MD simulations of many Class A GPCRs (including the Apelin receptor) supports the notion that these receptors explore active-like states in the absence of agonist binding. Taken together, and in the absence of data that supports agonist binding first, I think it is faulty logic to ascribe the agonist bound, G protein free state as a transition to the active state. It could be this, but it could also be a state that is not on the reaction pathway. Seed references are below: 1. Aranda-García, D., Stepniewski, T.M., Torrens-Fontanals, M. et al. Large scale investigation of GPCR molecular dynamics data uncovers allosteric sites and lateral gateways. Nat Commun 16, 2020 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57034-y 2. Kim TH, Chung KY, Manglik A, Hansen AL, Dror RO, Mildorf TJ, Shaw DE, Kobilka BK, Prosser RS. The role of ligands on the equilibria between functional states of a G protein-coupled receptor. J Am Chem Soc. 2013 Jun 26;135(25):9465-74. doi: 10.1021/ja404305k. Epub 2013 Jun 14. PMID: 23721409; PMCID: PMC3763947. 3. Nobles M, Benians A, Tinker A. Heterotrimeric G proteins precouple with G protein-coupled receptors in living cells. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2005 Dec 20;102(51):18706-11. doi: 10.1073/pnas.0504778102. Epub 2005 Dec 13. PMID: 16352729; PMCID: PMC1317907. 4. De Lean A, Stadel JM, Lefkowitz RJ. A ternary complex model explains the agonist-specific binding properties of the adenylate cyclase-coupled beta-adrenergic receptor. J Biol Chem. 1980 Aug 10;255(15):7108-17. PMID: 6248546. Figure 2 and supplementary figure 4. There are a number of relatively subtle changes in side chain position/rotation that are ascribed as being part of the activation pathway. The apparent resolution of the relevant parts of the receptor appears to be between 2 and 2.2A (supp fig 2 and 3), which should allow good confidence in assigning these. The maps on which these models are based and the models themselves are not provided (or perhaps I can’t find them?), so it is not possible as a reviewer to independently verify the side-chain movements being presented. I could not find an editorial policy on making these data (maps and models) available to reviewers, but this would be best-practice. Page 7, line 178. “Surprisingly, we observed ….”. No need for the pejorative surprising. Present the data and let the reader judge whether it is “surprising”. Page 7/8 lines 194-197. “These findings indicate that AMG986 can independently induce activation of a single protomer within the APLNR dimer, in contrast to JN241-9, which necessitates G-protein engagement for receptor activation.” These are snapshots of dynamic complexes and it is not clear that induced fit is in operation, I would encourage more cautious interpretation. I also note that if the authors interpretation is correct, one would predict that AMG986 would possess higher efficacy compared with JN241-9. I see no evidence of this. Pages 8 & 9. Section entitled: “G-protein coupled activation of APLNR facilitates the dimer-to-monomer transition” again, order of events is not known, it could be that dimer to monomer transition occurs first then G protein binding occurs then agonist binding occurs (or pretty much any other variation on this). Please apply a more cautious approach to interpretation OR provide evidence from an endogenous setting that supports one or other orders for the reaction pathway. Page 9, lines 236-240. “Furthermore, the kinetic GloSensor cAMP assay revealed that signaling response associated with monomeric activation (F101A) was greater than that of the dimeric form (WT) during the initial 15 minutes. However, both responses converged thereafter, further suggesting that most dimers transition into monomers upon receptor activation.” Please quantitate the difference in reaction rate and perform statistics to support that this. If this data quantitively and statistically supports faster cAMP inhibition kinetics if could be interpreted that the F101A mutant has higher propensity to pre-couple to its cognate G protein, thus increasing the agonist on-rate and subsequent Gi/o activation. Page 9, line 244. “Intriguingly, the ….” Please remove “intriguingly”. Page 10 & 11, section entitled “The extent of dimer dissociation upon APLNR activation is ligand-dependent”, once again, please apply a more conservative interpretation of the data. Page 10, lines 260-262. “These findings suggest that ligand-specific modulation of dimeric conformations may contributes to varying degrees of dimer dissociation upon activation.” Previously the authors imply that transition to the monomeric state enhances the rate of signalling, yet they do not assess whether the rate of signalling is differentially altered for the two ligands, which might be expected. Could the authors please comment? Figure 4c. The depletion of cholesterol from cells could conceivably alter availability of the G protein to the receptor and/or activity of adenylate cyclase (most isoforms are integral membrane proteins). As a minimum, the authors need to provide parallel experiments where the effect of cholesterol depletion on basal adenylate cyclase activity is assesses in cells that do not express the apelin receptor. Discussion should be rewritten with a more conservative interpretation of the data. I have been asked to comment on whether the authors have adequately addressed the comments by reviewer 2. On balance they have done a good job of this.

### Reviewer 4

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 5

I like to congratulate the authors for a very interesting and conclusive manuscript. All the concerns of Reviewer 2 have been addressed by the authors in their rebuttal letter. Except for the last point (how common might by the dimer/monomer transition observed for APLNR for class A and class B receptors?) the authors accordingly included changes in the manuscript. I would recommend adding a short statement in the discussion section addressing the above mentioned question. I enjoyed reading the manuscript and found only one additional point, not mentioned by the reviewers so far that in my opinion is so important that it needs clarification: To be sure that cholesterol depletion increases basal activity of APLNR it is necessary to show in the absence of APLNR how much cholesterol depletion affects forskolin-induced cAMP accumulation. Only if cholesterol depletion reduces cAMP accumulation to larger extent in APLNR expressing cells compared to non-APLNR expressing cells we can be sure that the results reflect an increase in basal activity of the receptor. Minor point: there is a little flaw in the figure legend of Fig. 4d: Dose-response curves for AMG986-induced cAMP accumulation in WT and F1013.24A….. If I’m correct, it should state: Concentration-response curves for the AMG986-mediated inhibition of forskolin-induced CAMP accumulations in WT and F1013.24A, …..

outcome_prediction.input:
You are a senior editor at Nature Communications.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.

Respond with EXACTLY one of these labels on the first line:
  major_revision
  minor_revision
  accept

Then provide a 2–3 sentence rationale explaining your prediction.

## Paper

## Abstract

G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are significant signal transducers that exist as monomers and in multiple oligomeric forms. However, molecular mechanism driving their dynamic interconversion to regulate intricate signaling in class A GPCRs remains elusive, compounding our understanding of their related pathophysiological functions. Here, we present a set of 12 assemblies of the apelin receptor (APLNR), including dimeric apo state, agonistic small molecule- or nanobody-bound state of monomeric and dimeric APLNR with and without G-proteins, providing a detailed dynamic view of the monomer-dimer transition. High-resolution cryo-EM structures reveal that different ligands induce varying degrees of pre-dissociation of dimers in the absence of G-protein, with G-protein coupling facilitating the transition from dimeric to monomeric receptor. These insights enhance our understanding of the dynamic regulation of class A GPCRs between monomeric and dimeric forms and advance the rational drug design strategies aimed at selectively modulating of APLNR signaling.

---

## Introduction

While Class C GPCRs are obligate dimers for their function, Class A GPCRs may exist as monomers or oligomers1-6, exhibiting distinct agonist affinity, efficacy, as well as the signaling profiles and pharmacological functions7-10. However, it remains unclear whether these forms mediate signaling transduction in an interconvertible manner or independently (Fig. 1a), compounding our understanding of complex mechanism of downstream signaling. Further studies on the molecular basis and functional implications of monomer–dimer interconversion in class A GPCRs are essential for achieving precise modulation of downstream signaling and understanding their pathophysiologic roles.

APLNR is a model system that may be suitable for investigating the dynamic transition between monomeric and dimeric forms of class A GPCR, supported by both transfected cell studies and cryo-EM structures4,11,12. However, these structures are inadequate for fully capturing the dynamics of the dimer-monomer transition, given their limited resolution and insufficient determination of multiple conformations. Moreover, the relationship between monomeric and dimeric forms and pathophysiologic functions has not been elucidated yet. APLNR is regard as a promising target due to its critical role in maintaining cardiovascular health and preventing muscle weakness13-18. Nonetheless, apelin-induced β-arrestin-dependent signaling contributes to detrimental cardiac hypertrophy, driving interests in the development of G-protein-biased APLNR agonists as potential heart failure therapies19-22. It is suggested that APLNR dimers exhibit distinct pathophysiological functions compared to monomers, indicating differences in the selective signaling pathways associated with various forms23-26. Therefore, it is crucial to elucidate how diverse ligands recognition induce the formation of specific monomeric or dimeric states, ultimately impacting signaling and therapeutic effects. AMG986, also named as BGE-105 and Azelaprag, is the most potent small molecule agonist in activating both G-protein and β-arrestin signaling of APLNR, advancing rapidly in clinical trials for anti-obesity treatment27-29. However, a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating AMG986 was recently discontinued owing to potential off-target liver toxicity. In parallel, JN241-9 stands as the pioneering single-domain antibody agonist targeting class A GPCR, derived from JN24130. The greater size of nanobody agonist contributes to the alignment of particles in cryo-EM data processing, overcoming micelle interference, thereby facilitating the capture of monomeric APLNR in the absence of G-protein. We have selected these two agonists to conduct a comprehensive study on the activation mechanisms and functions of dimers and monomers.

In this study, we resolved 12 cryo-EM density maps of wild type full-length APLNR, encompassing monomeric and dimeric forms of the apo state, agonists-bound state in the presence or absence of G-proteins, 9 of which achieve high resolution between 2.4 and 3.0 Å and enable the accurate structure modelling (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). These results reveal multiple conformational states of APLNR dimers and monomers, in both apo and active forms, which provide potential pathways for transitions between these states. Furthermore, our preliminary functional studies suggest a possible role of cholesterol in stabilizing the APLNR dimers, as well as how different ligands modulate the dimer-to-monomer transition, providing insights into drug development specifically targeting class A GPCRs between monomers and dimers.

## Results

Signaling and structural determination of APLNR dimers and monomers during activation process

Previous structural studies of the APLNR have indicated that the π-π interactions network formed by F1013.24 (where the superscript refers to the Ballesteros-Weinstein transmembrane numbering system31) plays a central role in stabilizing the dimeric interface11. To investigate the differences in downstream signaling mediated by monomeric and dimeric forms, we first assessed the signaling profile of wild type APLNR and the dimer-reduced form (FC1013.24A) using AMG986 and JN241-9, by conducting a NanoBiT assay and a GloSensor cAMP assay to detect G-protein activity and the bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) assay to detect β-arrestin recruitment. AMG986 showed roughly 10-fold greater potency in activating various G-proteins, including Gi, Gq and G13, as well as β-arrestin, compared to JN241-9 (Supplementary Figs. 1a-g). Additionally, AMG986 induced a more rapid activation rate than JN241-9 (Supplementary Fig. 1d). Though negligible differences in EC50 or Emax from G-protein signaling, the dimer-reduced form (F1013.24A) showed a higher Emax than the dimeric form in the β-arrestin signaling (Supplementary Fig. 1f), consistent with previous results11, which may be indicative that the dimer exhibits G-protein bias compared to the monomer. No detectable change in either Hill-slope or pEC50 is evident for either AMG986 or JN241-9 between dimers (WT) and the dimer-reduced form (F1013.24A), suggesting that ligand binding allostery, if present, is not detectable. Moreover, cAMP accumulation results showed that the dimer-reduced form appear to exhibit ~25% higher constitutive activity than that of dimeric form (Supplementary Figs. 1d-e, p < 0.001), prompting us to investigate the regulatory mechanism of dimerization induced by different potent ligands.

Determination of cryo-EM structures for class A GPCRs without G-protein is impeded by their small dimensions and inherent instability. Moreover, the crystallization process is rendered challenging when the structures exhibit flexibility, particularly when intermediate-state GPCRs manifest a diversity of conformations. Typically, receptors are often fused with proteins like BRIL to increase stability, which may not accurately represent their native conditions32,33. Here, we successfully achieved high-resolution cryo-EM structures of agonists-bound class A GPCR in various conformations without G-protein, providing potential insights into the dynamic process of activation. Specifically, dimeric receptors with increased size contributes significantly to achieve high-resolution structures in the absence of G-protein (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Figs. 1h-k). Furthermore, to overcome the difficulty of obtaining monomeric GPCR structures hindered by micelle interference, we selected JN241-9, a single-domain antibody, as an agonist suitable for structural alignment. The JN241-9–APLNR monomer species was identified during 2DA and 3D classification, albeit at relatively low resolution. Data processing statistics revealed a 5:1 ratio of dimer to monomer, with three distinct conformations of the JN241-9–dimer identified, differing only in the ligand-binding pose (termed by ligand-bound states LBS1a, LBS1b and LBS1c, respectively) (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 2a). Additionally, the two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein are distinguished by unique conformations of TM6 and helix 8 (H8) in one protomer (termed by LBS2a and LBS2b, respectively) (Supplementary Fig. 2b). These results indicate that the different ligands may induce different conformational states. Furthermore, we determined the structures of the APLNR–Gi1 complexes with the two agonists. Data processing statistics clearly demonstrate that monomeric complexes greatly exceed dimeric complexes, though dimeric formation is preferred in the absence of G-protein (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3), implying that most dimers have dissociated during activation. Notably, the two protomers are designated as protA and protB, respectively (Fig. 1b). Data processing revealed that AMG986-bound dimeric APLNR–Gi1 complexes adopt two conformations in protB (termed by ACT2a and ACT2b, respectively), aligning with those structures without G-protein (Supplementary Figs. 2b and 3b).

Ligands recognition and conformational comparison in different states

We first compared two AMG986-bound states of APLNR dimer without G-protein (LBS2a and LBS2b) against the apo state to identify structural differences (Fig. 2a). In both apo and AMG986–dimerLBS2a structures, the receptor adopts an inactive conformation, characterized by TM6 remaining in the closed state. In contrast to LBS2a, protB in LBS2b adopts an active-like conformation, with TM6 undergoing an outward movement and H8 bending inward to engage the intracellular pocket, in line with the previously reported fully active conformation (Fig. 2a)11. Our observations further reveal that protB progressively moves away from protA across the transition states from apo to LBS2b, represented by the movement of TM3 and TM4 in the intracellular half of protB when aligned with protA (Fig. 2b). While hydrophobic interactions involving the “FGTFF” motif (APLNR residues 97-101) contribute to dimeric stabilization in the extracellular half (Supplementary Fig. 4a), the intracellular half of the dimer interface might be stabilized by more extensive interactions mediated by cholesterol clusters, particularly involving TM1, TM2, and TM4 (Supplementary Fig. 4b). Cα distance measurements between TM1–TM4 residues of protB and nearby protA residues at the intracellular interface revealed a gradual increase from the apo state to LBS2b, with the most notable change at F782.53 (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Figs. 4c-f). These results suggest that in the absence of G-protein, APLNR dimers bound to ligands such as AMG986 exhibit a tendency to dissociate into monomers.

Upon comparing the ligand-binding pockets of the AMG986–dimer (LBS2a and LBS2b) and the AMG986–monomer–Gi complex, we noted that AMG986 in the protB of LBS2b adopts a similar binding pose to that in the AMG986–monomer–Gi complex (Fig. 2d). AMG986 in protB of LBS2b displays a lateral shift toward Y2997.43 relative to its position in LBS2a, thereby triggering a downward shift of key residues associated with activation, including F782.53, W2616.48 and Y2997.43, ultimately resulting the outward movement of TM6 in protB of LBS2b (Fig. 2d). Additionally, we observed three distinct conformations of JN241-9 as aforementioned, while the receptor remained unchanged in its inactive conformation. The pivotal residue Y105, located in the CDR3 region of nanobody JN241-9 and inserting into the very bottom of the ligand pocket, undergoes a rotation from pointing towards the crevice between TM4/5 and ECL2 of APLNR in the LBS1a conformation to facing the intracellular direction in the LBS1b conformation (Figs. 1b and 2e). When comparing the ligand-binding pockets of JN241-9–dimer with and without G-protein, we noted that in LBS 1b, the Y105 of JN241-9 is positioned closer to Y2997.43, resembling the fully active conformation. However, no alterations in key motifs or TM6 conformational changes were observed in LBS1b (Fig. 2e). In the fully active-state structure of JN241-9, Y105 exhibits a deeper insertion toward Y2997.43, facilitating the shift of F782.53, W2616.48 and Y2997.43 into their activation conformations. Furthermore, comparison of the ligand-binding pockets in protB showed that AMG986 penetrates more deeply than JN241-9, thereby driving the allosteric transition of F782.53, W2616.48 and Y2997.43, which could explain its capacity to induce the opening of TM6 (Fig. 2f). These findings indicate that AMG986 can independently induce one protomer within the APLNR dimer to adopt an active conformation, in contrast to JN241-9, which requires G-protein engagement to promote receptor activation. We also observed that the ligand engagement induced conformational changes of key motifs in receptors across the entire activation process, including the rearrangement of the “Na+ pocket”, “PVF motif”, “NPxxY motif”, “DRY motif”, which align with the known mechanisms of GPCR activation (Supplementary Fig. 5).

G-protein coupling promotes a dimer-to-monomer transition of APLNR

According to statistics and analysis of cryo-EM data processing, while two agonists-bound APLNR in the absence of G-protein exhibits more dimers than monomers, the proportion of monomer–G-protein complexes in the fully active state far exceeds dimer–G-protein complexes, indicating that most of dimers dissociate into monomers when introducing G-protein (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). The protB in JN241-9–dimer–Gi complex adopts an inactive-state configuration and H8 in protB is disordered. By comparing the contact areas between the receptor and the G-protein in monomeric complex and dimeric complex, we found that the buried surface area of monomer (1213 Å2) is significantly greater than that of dimer (917.7 Å2), suggesting that G-protein binding to the monomer is more stable (Fig. 3b). In addition, we compared JN241-9- and AMG986-bound dimerLBSb to their monomeric complex aligning with protA, and observed that the binding of heterotrimeric G-protein would generate a clash with protB in the dimerLBSb, therefore prompting the dissociation of protB (Fig. 3c).

Meanwhile, there are still a small fraction of cryo-EM particles corresponding to dimer–G-protein complexes, accounting for 1/14 of monomeric complexes activated by JN241-9 and 1/19 of monomeric complexes activated by AMG986 (Fig. 3a). The high-resolution structure of the JN241-9–dimer–Gi complex shows a 5.7-degree downward rotation of G-protein measured by αN helix to allow for the stable binding of protB. Notably, the position of the αN helix in the JN241-9–dimer–Gi complex closely resembles that observed in the apelin–dimer–Gi complex12 (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 7e). Additionally, cholesterol clusters at the dimerization interface were observed to elastically connect the two protomers like an adhesive sponge (Fig. 3d). Compared to the JN241-9-dimerLBS1b, the JN241-9–dimer–Gi complex exhibits a counterclockwise rotation of protB based on TM4 from the bottom view, which moves away from protA (Fig. 3d). The cholesterol density near TM1 is disorder in dimeric complex, resulting in a decreased protB-cholesterol interacting area of 1750 Å2 in the dimeric complex compared to that of 2031 Å2 in the JN241-9–dimerLBS1b, which suggest that protB tends to dissociate from protA when bound to G-protein (Fig. 3e). Furthermore, the kinetic GloSensor cAMP assay revealed that signaling response associated with monomeric activation (F101A) was greater than that of the dimeric form (WT) during the initial 15 minutes. However, both responses converged thereafter, further suggesting that most dimers transition into monomers upon receptor activation (Supplementary Fig. 1d).

Careful cryo-EM data processing of the JN241-9-bound APLNR–Gi1 complex identifies a class of dimers that were not bound to Gi-protein, from which we further uncover three distinct fractions of particles, whose conformations are consistent with the G-free specimens. The particle number ratios of these conformations change from 47.5% (LBS1a), 12.9% (LBS1b) and 39.6% (LBS1c) to 27.6%, 17.1% and 55.3%, respectively. The increasement of the proportions of LBS1b and LBS1c states further indicates that these two conformations are closer to the active state conformation in comparison with LBS1a state (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Figs. 2a and 3a).

The extent of dimer dissociation upon APLNR activation is ligand-dependent

Different from JN241-9, the sole action of AMG986 without G-protein is capable of achieving the partial activation of one protomer in the APLNR dimer, thus prompting a tendency for the protomers to dissociate from each other (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 4). Inspiringly, the structures of AMG986–dimer–Gi complexes adopt either the active or the inactive conformations in protB, aligning with those dimeric structures in the absence of G-protein (Supplementary Fig. 6a). These findings suggest that ligand-specific modulation of dimeric conformations may contributes to varying degrees of dimer dissociation upon activation.

Comparison of the AMG986–dimerLBS2b with the monomeric complex reveal that the binding of G-protein would generate a more severe clash between Gβγ in the monomeric complex and H8 as well as ICL1 of protB in the AMG986–dimerLBS2b, compared to the JN241-9-bound APLNR structures (Fig. 3c). This implies that the AMG986-bound dimer has a higher propensity to dissociate during activation than the JN241-9-bound dimer. Additionally, comparing the two agonists-bound dimeric complexes highlights a counterclockwise rotation of about 27° in the entire G heterotrimer observed in the AMG986-bound structure (Supplementary Fig. 6b).

To date, multiple agonist-bound APLNR dimer structures in the presence or absence of Gi-protein have been resolved11,12. Accordingly, we compared the APLNR structures resolved in this study with previously reported structures. Pairwise alignment of the entire dimeric assemblies revealed relatively small Cα root mean square deviation (RMSD) values (<1.0 Å) among G-protein-free dimers (Supplementary Fig. 7a). In contrast, Cα RMSDs between structures with and without G-protein coupling exhibited larger deviations (1.0 to 2.5 Å), largely attributable to conformational shifts in TM6 and H8 (Supplementary Fig. 7a). Moreover, Cα RMSDs among G-protein-coupling dimers also showed relatively larger deviations (1.0 to 2.1 Å), suggesting that different ligands induce distinct dimer conformations in the active state (Supplementary Fig. 7a). To assess the extent of dimer dissociation, we compared the Cα RMSDs of protB aligned on protA (Supplementary Fig. 7b). Comparison between G-protein-bound and G-protein-free dimers revealed a remarkably wide range of Cα RMSDs (2.3 to 6.3 Å), particularly in comparisons involving the ELA–Gi complex (PDB: 7W0N)11, further indicating different ligands induce varying degrees of dimer dissociation during activation (Supplementary Figs. 7b-d).
