## Methods

Constructs

To prepare the cryo-EM sample of AMG986- and JN241-9-bound APLNR without G-protein, human wild type full-length APLNR (UniProt: P35414) was cloned into pFastBac1 vector (Invitrogen) with an N-terminal hemagglutinin (HA) signal sequence connected to a Flag tag. To further improve APLNR expression, a thermostabilized BRIL was fused to the N-terminus after the Flag-tag. A double MBP tag followed by a C-terminal His tag was fused into the C terminal of APLNR with a linker containing a TEV protease cleavage site. Unlike the construct for JN241-9-bound APLNR, LgBit was added at the end of TEV protease site in the construct of AMG986-bound APLNR. To prepare the cryo-EM sample of AMG986- and JN241-9-bound APLNR–Gi1 complexes, an N-terminal HA signal sequence connected to a Flag-tag was fused to the N-terminal APLNR. Human dominant-negative (DN) Gαi1 was generated by site-directed mutagenesis to decrease the nucleotide-binding affinity and increase the stability of G-protein60. Human Gβ1 was cloned into pFastBac dual vector with Gγ2. In addition, the scFv16, which encodes the single-chain variable fragment of mAb16, was subcloned into pFastBac plasmid.

To analyze G-protein signaling through NanoBit assay and cAMP accumulation assay, a Flag-tag was fused to the N-terminal of full-length and various mutants of APLNR. Additionally, Gαi1 was fused with LgBit, and Gγ was fused with SmBiT, and all three constructs were cloned into pcDNA3.1 plasmids. For β-arrestin signaling analysis, the C-terminus of the APLNR receptor was fused with the Rluc8 fragment, the Venus fragment was inserted into the N-terminus of β-arrestin2 and then both were cloned into pBiT1.1 plasmids (Promega).

Expression and purification of scFv16

The secreted scFv16 protein was expressed and purified using the bac-to-bac system. Briefly, the scFv16 with a C-terminal histidine-tag was overexpressed in Trichoplusia ni Hi5 insect cells for 48 h and purified by Ni-NTA resin. The eluted protein was cleaved by 3C protease and further purified by gel filtration chromatography using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare). The purified scFv16 fractions were concentrated and stored at -80 °C until use.

Expression and purification of JN241-9

JN241-9 with a 6× His tag at the C-terminal was expressed in the periplasm of E. coli BL21 cells. Briefly, JN241-9 target gene was transformed in the bacterium and amplified in TB culture medium. When OD600 reached 0.7-1.2, 1 mM IPTG was added to induce expression followed by overnight incubation at 28 °C. JN241-9 was purified by Ni-NTA resin. The eluted protein was collected and then desalted using a HiPrep 26/10 Desalting column. Fractions of JN241-9 were concentrated to ~8 mg/ml and quickly frozen in the liquid nitrogen with 10% glycerol and stored at −80 °C.

Expression and purification of agonists-APLNR

APLNR constructs were expressed in sf9 insect cells using the bac-to-bac Baculovirus Expression System (Invitrogen). The cells were then incubated for 48 h at 27 °C and subsequently collected by centrifugation at 1,000 × g for 30 min. Cell precipitates were stored at -80 °C until further use. The cell pellets were suspended in buffer containing 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 2 mM MgCl2, 100 mM NaCl, protease inhibitor cocktail (Bimake) and agonist (100 nM AMG986 or 1 μM JN241-9). The membranes were solubilized with 0.5% (w/v) lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) and 0.1% (w/v) cholesterol hemisuccinate (CHS) for 2 h at 4 °C and separated by centrifugation at 30,000g for 30 min. Following incubation with amylose resin (NEB), and the protein was eluted with 20 mM maltose. TEV protease was then added for 1 h to remove the 2×MBP protein. After concentrated, the protein was loaded onto Superose 6 Increase 10/ 300 GL (GE Healthcare) column with running buffer containing 20 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 0.00075% (w/v) LMNG, 0.00025% (w/v) glyco-diosgenin (GDN), 0.0002% (w/v) CHS and agonist (100 nM AMG986 or 1 μM JN241-9). The monomeric peak fractions were collected and concentrated to 10-15 mg/ml for electron microscopy experiments.

Expression and purification of agonists–APLNR–Gi1 Complexes

APLNR, Gαi1 and Gβγ constructs were co-expressed at the ratio of 1:1:1 in sf9 insect cells using the bac-to-bac Baculovirus Expression System (Invitrogen). The cells were then incubated for 48 h at 27 °C and subsequently collected by centrifugation at 1,000 × g for 30 min. For the purification of APLNR–Gi1 complexes, the cell pellets were suspended in buffer containing 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 2 mM MgCl2, 100 mM NaCl and protease inhibitor cocktail (Bimake), followed by addition of 1.2 mg scFv16 antibody, 12 mU/ml apyrase (Sigma), and agonist (100 nM AMG986 or 1 μM JN241-9). The mixture was incubated for 1 h at room temperature for complex formation. After that, the membranes were solubilized with 0.5% (w/v) LMNG and 0.1% (w/v) CHS for 2 h at 4 °C. The supernatant was then separated by centrifugation at 30,000g for 30 min. Following incubation with anti-FLAG affinity resin, the protein was eluted with 0.2 mg/ml Flag peptide. Add 10% (w/w) scFv16 antibody and incubated for 15 min at room temperature. The elution was concentrated with a 100 kDa cut-off concentrator (Millipore) and loaded onto a Superose 6 increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare) with a running buffer containing 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 0.00075% LMNG, 0.0002% (w/v) CHS, 0.00025% (w/v) GDN and agonist (100 nM AMG986 or 1 μM JN241-9). The monomeric peak fractions were collected and concentrated to 10-15 mg/ml for electron microscopy experiments.

Cryo-EM grid preparation and data collection

To prepare cryo-EM grids, purified complexes (3 μL, ~10 mg/ml) were applied individually to the grids that were subsequently flash frozen in liquid ethane using Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific) under 100% humidity at 4 C. For AMG986-, JN241-9-bound APLNR and AMG986-, JN241-9-bound APLNR–Gi1 complexes, cryo-EM data collection was performed on a Titan Krios at 300 kV accelerating voltage. Micrographs were recorded using a Falcon 4 direct electron detector in super-resolution mode with a pixel size of 0.93 Å using EPU software. Image stacks were obtained at a dose rate of about 13.24 electrons per Å2 per second with a defocus ranging from -1.0 to -2.5 μm. The total exposure time was 3.92 s, and 40 frames were recorded per micrograph.

Cryo-EM data processing

Dose-fractionated image stacks were aligned using MotionCor2.161, implemented in Relion 4.0. Contrast transfer function (CTF) parameters for each micrograph were estimated by Gctf v1.1862. The following data processing was performed using RELION 4.0 and CryoSPARC v4.0.363,64.

For the JN241-9-bound APLNR complex, a total of 13,193,854 particles were auto-picked in Relion 4.0. High-quality particle projections from multiple rounds of 2D classification and Heterogenous Refinement were utilized for ab-initio reconstruction to generate initial reference maps. A good subset of 2,817,890 particle projections was subjected to Heterogenous Refinement and 2D classification and two distinct particle populations were discerned, corresponding to the APLNR monomer and APLNR dimer. A subsequent round of 3D classification for APLNR dimer yielded three particle subsets: JN241-9-dimerLBS1a, JN241-9–dimerLBS1b and JN241-9–dimerLBS1c. These subsets of 97,020 particles, 101,362 particles and 138,605 particles were subjected to 3D refinement, CTF refinement, and Bayesian polishing in Relion, generating three maps with a global resolution of 2.7 Å.

For the AMG986-bound APLNR complex, a total of 14,104,471 particles were auto-picked. Particles from multiple rounds of 2D classification and Heterogenous Refinement were utilized for ab-initio reconstruction to generate initial reference maps. A good subset of 2,271,602 particle projections was subjected to Heterogenous Refinement and 2D classification, identifying APLNR monomer and APLNR dimer populations. Further 3D classification yielded two particle subsets: AMG-dimerLBS2a and AMG-dimerLBS2b. These subsets of 306,883 particles and 288,225 particles were subjected to 3D refinement, CTF refinement, and Bayesian polishing in Relion, generating two maps with a global resolution of 2.4 Å for AMG–dimerLBS2a and 2.5 Å for AMG–dimerLBS2b.

For the JN241-9-bound APLNR–Gi1 complex, a total of 16,153,222 particles were auto-picked. Particles from multiple rounds of 2D classification and Heterogenous Refinement were utilized for ab-initio reconstruction to generate initial reference maps. 4,170,567 particles were subjected to Heterogenous Refinement and 2D classification and four distinct particle populations were discerned: JN241-9–monomer, JN241-9–dimer JN241-9–monomer–Gi and JN241-9–dimer–Gi. A subsequent round of 3D classification for JN241-9–dimer also yielded three particle subsets: LBS1a, LBS1b and LBS1c. Final subsets of 187,827 particles for JN241-9–monomer–Gi and 198,168 particles for JN241-9–dimer–Gi were subjected to 3D refinement, CTF refinement, and Bayesian polishing in Relion, generating two maps with a global resolution of 2.5 Å and 3.0 Å, respectively.

For the AMG986-bound APLNR–Gi1 complex, a total of 6,477,441 particles were auto-picked. Particles from 2D classification and Heterogenous Refinement were utilized for ab-initio reconstruction to generate initial reference maps. A good subset of 1,257,292 particle projections was subjected to Heterogenous Refinement and 2D classification and four populations were discerned: AMG986–monomer, AMG986–dimer AMG986–monomer–Gi and AMG986–dimer–Gi. The final subset of 63,229 particles for AMG986–monomer–Gi were subjected to 3D refinement, CTF refinement, and Bayesian polishing in Relion, generating a map with a global resolution of 2.8 Å.

Comprehensive refinement metrics are detailed in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

Model building and refinement

The model of Apelin receptor in complex with single-domain antibody (PDB: 6KNM) was used to generate the initial template of receptor30. The atomic coordinates of Gi and scFv16 from the structure of MM07-bound APLNR–Gi1 complex (PDB: 8XZH) were used to generate the initial template of the G-protein complex19. Models were docked into the cryo-EM density map using UCSF Chimera65. Agonist coordinates and geometry restraints were generated using a phenix.elbow66. The docked model was subjected to flexible fitting using Rosetta 2019.35 and iterative manual adjustment in Coot and real-space-refined in Phenix67. The final refinement statistics were validated using the module ‘comprehensive validation (cryo-EM)’ in Phenix66. The goodness-of-fit of the model to the map was determined using a global model-versus-map Fourier shell correlation. The refinement statistics are provided in supplementary information. Structural figures were created using UCSF Chimera and the UCSF Chimera X package65,68.

NanoBiT-G-protein dissociation assay

G-protein activation was measured using a NanoBiT G-protein dissociation assay.2 HEK293T cells were seeded in a 6-well plate and plasmid transfection was performed with a mixture of 600 ng Gαi, 500 ng Sm-Gβ, 500 ng Gγ2, 200 ng APLNR plasmid (per well). After 6 h of transfection, cells were digested and resuspended in complete DMEM medium (5% FBS, 1% antibiotic) and plated in 96-well flat-bottomed white microplates at a volume of 100 μl per well. Next day, the cells were washed twice with D-PBS and incubated in 40 μl of 5 μM coelenterazine A solution diluted with HBSS (assay buffer) for 40 min at room temperature. After baseline luminescence was measured for 3 cycles (Tecan), test ligands (5×, diluted in the HBSS assay buffer) were added to the cells (10 μl per well) and incubated for 3-5 min at room temperature before the second measurement was taken. The ligand-induced signal ratio was normalized to the baseline luminescence, and fold-change signals over vehicle treatment were used to show the G-protein dissociation response. Concentration-response curves were fitted using the “log (agonist) vs. response (Three parameters)” model in GraphPad Prism 8 to obtain EC₅₀ values.

cAMP accumulation assay

Human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK293T) cells were seeded in a 6-well plate and transfected with a plasmid mixture consisting of 1,500 ng receptor and 500 ng cAMP biosensor GloSensor-22F (Promega). After 6 h, transfected cells were plated onto a 96-well plate. After another 12 h, cells were washed twice with D-PBS and then incubated in CO2-independent media (assay buffer) containing 2% GloSensor cAMP Reagent (Promega) and 1 μM Forskolin at a volume of 40 μl per well. MβCD with various concentrations was added to assay buffer when investigating the stabilized effect of cholesterols. The transfected cells were incubated for 30 min in 37 °C CO2 incubator and another 30 min at room temperature in the dark before measurements for baseline luminescence (Spark Multimode microplate reader, TECAN). Next, test ligands (5×, diluted in CO2-independent media containing 1 μM Forskolin) were added to the cells (10 μl per well) and incubated for 15-20 min at room temperature before the second measurement was taken. Concentration-response curves were fitted using the “log (agonist) vs. response (Three parameters)” model in GraphPad Prism 8 to obtain EC₅₀ values.

Bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) assay

BRET assay was used to detect β-arrestin recruitment. HEK293T cells were transiently co-transfected with APLNR-Rluc8 and Venus-β-arrestin2 (1:4). The transfected cells were seeded into 96-well flat-bottomed white microplates at a volume of 100 μl per well. After 24 h, cells were washed twice with D-PBS and then maintained in the BRET buffer (containing 10 mM HEPES and 0.1% BSA) at a volume of 45 ml per well for 30 min in 37 °C CO2 incubator. Luciferase substrate coelenterazine h (5 μM) was then added to the transfected cells. Coelenterazine and cells were incubated together in the dark for 10 min and the plate was placed into the microplate reader to read the base value. Transfected cells were then stimulated with ligands (5 μl) at different concentrations and read with the microplate reader again to get the BRET signal value. Both the BRET signal value and the base value were determined as the ratio of light emitted by Venus-tagged biosensors and light emitted by Rluc8-tagged biosensors. The BRET acceptor (520-560 nm) and BRET donor (460-485 nm) emission signals were measured using the Spark Multimode microplate reader (Tecan). Venus’s fluorescence was measured before reading luminescence and calculated as average fluorescence from each control well. The BRET signal from the same well was determined as the ratio of the light emitted by Venus (520-560 nm) over that emitted by RLuc8 (460-485 nm). Concentration-response curves were fitted using the “log (agonist) vs. response (Three parameters)” model in GraphPad Prism 8 to obtain EC₅₀ values.

Cell-surface ELISA

Membrane expression of APLNR was determined by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to detect the N-terminal Flag tag on the WT and mutants transiently expressed in HEK293T cells. After transfection, cells were seeded into 96-well flat-bottomed white microplates at a volume of 100 μl per well. After 24 h, cells were washed twice with PBS and fixed with 4% formaldehyde for 10 min followed by three times washing with PBS. Then cells were incubated with blocking buffer (1% BSA in PBS) for 1 h at room temperature. Afterwards, cells were incubated with anti-FLAG M2 HRP-conjugated monoclonal antibody (Sigma Aldrich) in blocking buffer for 30 min at room temperature. After washing three times with PBS, 80 μl/well diluent SuperSignal Elisa Femto Maximum Sensitivity Substrate (ThermoFisher Scientific) was added. This manuscript is potentially a very exciting study delving into the molecular interactions of Apelin receptor 1 dimerization and it's links to function. The beauty of realtime sensors like the GloSensor is they provide kinetic information, yet the assays were not performed to collect such information (Eg single time readings after 20 min incubation of ligand). From their analysis in S4 it looks like the NPxxY motif is the one that shows the biggest difference in terms of apo to active state, can the others comment on this as this appears to be away from any dimer interface. Why the big changes compared to some of the other key motifs? Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comments. An analysis of 234 structures from 45 class A GPCRs in previous studies revealed a common activation mechanism that integrates key motifs (CWxP, PIF, Na⁺ pocket, NPxxY and DRY) into a unified conformational pathway2. This pathway operates through four hierarchical layers (Fig. R13): Layer 1: Signal Initiation. Agonist binding disrupts Na⁺-coordinated residues (D2.50, S3.39, N7.45), triggering inward movement of TM7, and residues at TM3 (3.40) and TM6 (6.44, 6.48) repack, initiating outward movement of TM6’s cytoplasmic end. Layer 2: Hydrophobic Lock Opening. Breaking of hydrophobic contacts (PIF motif) between TM3, TM5 and TM6, releasing TM6. Meanwhile, W6.48 rotation destabilizes TM6, facilitating its outward shift. Layer 3: Microswitch Rewiring. Y7.53 loses contacts with TM1/helix 8 and forms new bonds with TM3 (R3.50, I3.46), strengthening TM3-TM7 coupling. TM7 inward movement further displaces TM6 (NPxxY motif). Layer 4: G-Protein Coupling. Ionic lock (DRY motif) breaks, releasing R3.50. This residue engages Gα, while TM6’s outward shift creates a G-protein binding cavity. In summary, activation of GPCRs involves a conserved conformational rearrangement of key motifs, resulting in the outward displacement of TM6. Concurrently, TM7 moves inward to stabilize the active conformation of TM6. The NPxxY motif, situated at the intracellular end of TM7, exhibits the largest structural transition from the apo to the active state among all conserved motifs. Reply figure 13. Common activation pathway of class A GPCRs2. Four layers were qualitatively defined based on the topology of the pathway and their roles in activation: signal initiation (layer 1), signal propagation (layer 2), microswitches rewiring (layer 3) and G-protein coupling (layer 4). 8. Homo dimers are reported to form for lots of class A receptors and B receptors, can they authors comment how common their findings might be? Response: Thank you for your comments. While class C GPCRs are known to mediate signaling only in a dimeric form, class A and class B GPCRs were initially believed to function exclusively as monomers. However, evidence supporting dimerization in class A and class B receptors emerged with the development of advanced techniques such as photoaffinity labeling and cross-linking, which identified homodimers of β -adrenergic 2 receptor and heterodimers between cholecystokinin-8 (CCK-8) and dopamine (DA) receptors3,4. The existence of GPCR dimers is now well supported by a range of biochemical approaches, including epitope-tagging, immunoprecipitation, FRET and BRET assays. In class A GPCRs, several homodimer forms have been validated through these approaches: β₂-adrenergic receptor (β₂-AR), somatostatin receptor 5 (SSTR5), and δ-/κ-opioid receptors5; AT1R and A₂AR6; CCR2 and CCR57; apelin receptor8, and M₃ muscarinic receptor (M₃R)9. In addition, functionally relevant heterodimers have also been reported, such as the dopamine D₁ receptor and adenosine A₁ receptor complex10. Class B GPCRs also exhibit dimerization and oligomerization properties. GLP-1R has been confirmed to form homodimers through multiple resonance energy transfer assays, with TM4 identified as the interface of the dimeric interaction11. ECD-mediated oligomerization of PTH1R was similarly confirmed in living cells using BRET and FRET techniques12. Additionally, the GIPR has been shown to suppress PAC1 receptor-driven neuronal differentiation through heterocomplex formation13. Powerful advances in single-molecule microscopy have facilitated the measurements of the dynamic process of GPCR dimerization in real time. Homodimerization has been frequently reported for several class A GPCRs using various techniques: spot intensity analysis (APLNR, β AR, β AR, M R, FPR, D R)8,14- 1 2 1 3 17; photobleach step counting (μOR, PAFR, M R)18-20, and two-color coincidence 2 detection (S1P3R, mCannR2)21,22. These studies indicate that the dimeric formation of the receptor is transient and density-dependent. TIRFM is particularly suitable for assessing these dynamic membrane processes and quantifying oligomeric states. For example, at densities below 0.3 receptor particles/μm², ~60% of APLNR and ~44% of PAFR molecules formed dimers or oligomers. In class B GPCRs, CRF1R has shown a stable monomer/dimer equilibrium both at the plasma membrane and in the ER, as revealed by TIRFM23. The frequency and relevance of GPCR dimerization in vivo remains under debate. Some findings are derived from receptor overexpression systems, which may introduce experimental artifacts. Advanced imaging tools, such as super-resolution microscopy, can further surpasses the diffraction limit, offering quantitative insights into the stoichiometry of receptor oligomers. Given the limited structural understanding of class A and class B GPCR dimers, our study provides additional evidence supporting the existence of APLNR homodimer and elucidates a dynamic monomer–dimer transition mechanism that contributes to a deeper understanding of complex downstream signaling.
